## Example

Take the theorem's external metric with a constant conformal factor $\Omega=b>0$, so $g=b^2\eta$. The scalar field is smeared by $\Phi_g(f)=\Phi_0(b^3f)$ relative to $d\mathrm{vol}_g=b^4d^4x$. In particular, $R_g=0$ and $P_g=b^{-2}\Box_\eta$. Relative to $d\mathrm{vol}_g(x)d\mathrm{vol}_g(y)$, the two-point kernel is $W_g(x,y)=b^{-2}W_0(x,y)$, so its double smearing is $b^6$ times the flat covariance. This example checks the constant-factor normalization only; it asserts no preferred state for a general curved metric.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, a positive constant $b$, and the selected massless field construction of [[thm-qft-conformal-external-scalar]].

[A1] $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is the countable-choice assumption of [[def-countable-choice]]; it is inherited from the conditional QFT and EMG supplier chains.

[F1] [[thm-qft-conformal-external-scalar]]: $R_g=-6\Omega^{-3}\Box_\eta\Omega$ and $P_g(\Omega^{-1}u)=\Omega^{-3}\Box_\eta u$ for smooth $u$.

[F2] [[thm-qft-conformal-external-scalar]]: for every compact test $f$, $\Phi_g(f)=\Phi_0(\Omega^3f)$.

[F3] [[thm-qft-conformal-external-scalar]]: relative to $d\mathrm{vol}_g(x)d\mathrm{vol}_g(y)$, $W_g(x,y)=\Omega(x)^{-1}\Omega(y)^{-1}W_0(x,y)$.

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Since $\partial_a b=0$, $\Box_\eta b=0$ and [F1] gives $R_g=0$. Also $g^{ab}=b^{-2}\eta^{ab}$ and $d\mathrm{vol}_g=b^4d^4x$, so the density definition gives $\Box_g=b^{-2}\Box_\eta$ and hence $P_g=b^{-2}\Box_\eta$. [given, A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 Substituting $\Omega=b$ into [F2] gives $\Phi_g(f)=\Phi_0(b^3f)$; [F3] gives the relative kernel $W_g=b^{-2}W_0$. In the double smearing the two volume factors contribute $b^4b^4$, so the total coefficient is $b^{-2}b^8=b^6$, exactly the coefficient from the two test multipliers $b^3b^3$. [given, A1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 At $b=1$ these formulas reduce to the flat metric, field, and covariance. Locality is inherited from the theorem and is not checked here; this example checks only the stated normalization and does not assert uniqueness of a vacuum on a nonconstant curved metric. [given, F2, F3, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]] and the mathematical free Dirac data of [[def-qft-dirac-projections]], [[lem-qft-dirac-projection-matrices]], and [[lem-qft-free-dirac-car-locality]]. Let $G=\mathbb R^4\rtimes SO^+(1,3)$ act by $x\mapsto a+\Lambda x$, with product $(a_2,\Lambda_2)(a_1,\Lambda_1)=(a_2+\Lambda_2a_1,\Lambda_2\Lambda_1)$. Let $\widetilde G$ be the subgroup of triples $(a,\Lambda,S)$ generated by translations $(a,I,I)$ and the explicit rotation/boost triples $(0,R_{\mathbf n}(\theta),S_R(\theta))$ and $(0,B_{\mathbf n}(\chi),S_B(\chi))$ of [[lem-qft-dirac-projection-matrices]], with product $(a_2,\Lambda_2,S_2)(a_1,\Lambda_1,S_1)=(a_2+\Lambda_2a_1,\Lambda_2\Lambda_1,S_2S_1)$ and the subspace topology from $\mathbb R^4\times M_4(\mathbb R)\times GL(4,\mathbb C)$. Its projection onto $G$ is surjective by [[lem-qft-lorentz-boost-rotation-factorization]]. For $\tilde g=(a,\Lambda,S)$ define the spinor test pullback
$$\tau_{\tilde g}F(x)=(S^{-1})^\dagger F(\Lambda^{-1}(x-a)).$$
The fermionic Fock space of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]] carries a strongly continuous unitary representation $U$ of $\widetilde G$ such that
$$U(\tilde g)\Psi(F)U(\tilde g)^{-1}=\Psi(\tau_{\tilde g}F).$$
Let $\mathcal A_D^{\mathrm{gr}}$ be the algebra generated by all bounded $\Psi(F)$ and $\Psi(F)^\dagger$ for Schwartz spinor tests $F$. The vacuum $\Omega$ is invariant and cyclic for $\mathcal A_D^{\mathrm{gr}}$. A $2\pi$ spatial spin rotation acts as $(-1)^N$ on the $n$-particle sector with value $(-1)^n$; a $4\pi$ rotation acts as the identity. The translation generators and joint spectral measure are those of [[lem-qft-dirac-fermionic-translation-spectrum]], so the joint spectrum is contained in the closed future cone, the zero-energy eigenspace is $\mathbb C\Omega$, and for $\mu>0$ the nonvacuum energy has gap at least $\mu$. The first-quantized $h_D$ has both signs of energy; this Fock-space generator is a different operator on a different Hilbert space. No general spin-statistics theorem or local cyclicity claim is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The fixed spinor test convention $\int F^\dagger\Psi$, the shell phase $p\circ x=\omega x^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x$, explicit matrix lifts, proper orthochronous Lorentz geometry, and the actual draft supplier interfaces recorded below.

[A1] Countable Choice is the choice strength assumed for the completed Fock spaces. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] The Clifford matrices, $h_D$, $P_\pm$, particle and conjugate negative-energy subspaces, and the second-variable-linear pairing are those of [[def-qft-dirac-projections]]. By [[lem-qft-dirac-projection-matrices]], the matrix fields $P_\pm$ are bounded complementary orthogonal projections and their ranges $\mathcal H_\pm$ are closed separable Hilbert subspaces.

[F2] The explicit $S_R,S_B$ obey $S\Gamma(p)S^{-1}=\Gamma(\Lambda p)$ and $S\beta S^\dagger=\beta$; each proper orthochronous $\Lambda$ factors into one boost and one rotation. [[lem-qft-dirac-projection-matrices]] [[lem-qft-lorentz-boost-rotation-factorization]]

[F3] The future mass shell is $p=(\omega(\mathbf k),\mathbf k)$ with $d\nu_\mu=d^3\mathbf k/((2\pi)^3 2\omega)$, and this measure is invariant under every proper orthochronous Lorentz map. [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]] [[lem-qft-mass-shell-measure-invariant]]

[F4] The free Dirac field is the bounded smeared CAR field defined by $\Psi(F)=c(P_+u_F)+c^\dagger(\overline{P_-u_F})$; $F\mapsto u_F$ is continuous from Schwartz space to $\mathcal H_D$, and its separate positive and negative kernels are the Fourier distributions $C_+$ and $C_-$ displayed there, with tested pairings $\langle P_+u_F,P_+u_G\rangle$ and $\langle P_-u_F,P_-u_G\rangle$. [[lem-qft-free-dirac-car-locality]]

[F5] The antisymmetric Fock sectors, finite-particle domain, creation formulas, and CAR relations use the conventions of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]] and [[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]. By [[lem-qft-dirac-projection-matrices]], $\mathcal H_\pm$ are separable, so their finite direct sum $\mathcal K=\mathcal H_+\oplus\overline{\mathcal H_-}$ is separable (take pairs from countable dense sets); with Countable Choice [A1], the hypotheses of the CAR supplier hold for $H=\mathcal K$.

[F6] Smooth compactly supported vector functions are dense in $L^2$ on an open Euclidean set, componentwise. [[lem-smooth-compactly-supported-functions-are-dense-in-ltwo-of-an-open-set]]

[F7] The exact fermionic translation phases, maximal generator domains, joint PVM, forward-cone support, vacuum eigenspace and mass gap are established in [[lem-qft-dirac-fermionic-translation-spectrum]].

[F8] In the fixed inertial coordinates of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], proper orthochronous Lorentz matrices satisfy $\Lambda^T\eta_0\Lambda=\eta_0$, have determinant $+1$, and preserve the chosen future cone, as defined in [[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]. The matrix group $SO^+(1,3)$ is closed under products and inverses by [[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

[F9] The quarter-turn values give $\cos\pi=-1$, $\sin\pi=0$, $\cos2\pi=1$, and $\sin2\pi=0$. [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]]

## Proof



1.1 For translations the identities $S\Gamma(p)S^{-1}=\Gamma(\Lambda p)$ and $S\beta S^\dagger=\beta$ hold because $S=I$ and $\Lambda=I$. They hold for each explicit rotation and boost generator by [F2]. They are preserved under products: if they hold for $(\Lambda_1,S_1)$ and $(\Lambda_2,S_2)$, then $(S_2S_1)\Gamma(p)(S_2S_1)^{-1}=\Gamma(\Lambda_2\Lambda_1p)$ and $(S_2S_1)\beta(S_2S_1)^\dagger=\beta$. They are also preserved under inverses, since $S^{-1}\Gamma(r)S=\Gamma(\Lambda^{-1}r)$ follows by setting $p=\Lambda^{-1}r$ in the first identity, and $S^{-1}\beta S^{-\dagger}=\beta$ follows by multiplying the second identity by $S^{-1}$ and $S^{-\dagger}$. Thus both identities hold for every element of the subgroup $\widetilde G$ generated by the stated triples. Now for $p=(\omega,\mathbf k)$ the projection identity in [F1] gives $P_+(\mathbf k)\beta=(\Gamma(p)+\mu)/(2\omega)$. For $q=(\omega,-\mathbf k)$ it gives $P_-(\mathbf k)\beta=(\Gamma(q)-\mu)/(2\omega)$. Thus, using $d\nu_\mu=d^3\mathbf k/((2\pi)^3 2\omega)$, the separate kernels in [F4] are $$C_+(z)=\int(\Gamma(p)+\mu)\beta e^{-ip\circ z}\,d\nu_\mu(p),\qquad C_-(z)=\int(\Gamma(q)-\mu)\beta e^{+iq\circ z}\,d\nu_\mu(q),$$ where $p\circ z=p^0z^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf z$ and both $p,q$ range over the future mass shell. The matrix relations now established for every $\tilde g\in\widetilde G$, together with $S^{-1}\beta=\beta S^\dagger$, give $S(\Gamma(p)\pm\mu)\beta S^\dagger=(\Gamma(\Lambda p)\pm\mu)\beta$. In each shell integral, change variables $r=\Lambda p$ (or $r=\Lambda q$); invariance of $d\nu_\mu$ [F3] and $(\Lambda p)\circ z=p\circ(\Lambda^{-1}z)$ show $C_\pm(\Lambda z)=S C_\pm(z)S^\dagger$. The coefficients grow at most linearly on the shell, so these Fourier integrals define tempered distributions and their pairings with Schwartz tests converge. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F8, algebra, construct]

2.1 For $F,G\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb C^4)$, [F4] identifies $\langle P_+u_F,P_+u_G\rangle$ and $\langle P_-u_F,P_-u_G\rangle$ with the respective kernel pairings $\int F(x)^\dagger C_\pm(x-y)G(y)\,d^4x\,d^4y$. Set $F'=\tau_{\tilde g}F$ and $G'=\tau_{\tilde g}G$. In each pairing, the spin factors are $S^{-1}$ and $S^{-\dagger}$; changing variables $x=a+\Lambda x'$, $y=a+\Lambda y'$ has unit Jacobian, cancels the translation in $x-y$, and the kernel identity of step 1.1 cancels both spin factors. Hence both polarized one-particle pairings are preserved, and the maps $P_\pm u_F\mapsto P_\pm u_{F'}$ are well-defined isometries on their test-generated subspaces. Applying the inverse group element proves they are onto after completion. For the conjugate negative-energy sector, conjugating the same preserved pairing and reversing its arguments gives the corresponding isometry on $\overline{\mathcal H_-}$. [F3, F4, F8, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The test-generated subspaces are dense. For $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\};\mathbb C^4)$, $P_\pm u$ is smooth and compactly supported away from the massless apex; such projected vectors are dense in $\mathcal H_\pm$ by [F1] and [F6], since removing the single point does not change an $L^2$ class. Choose $g\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ with $\int g(t)dt=1$ and set $\widehat F(t,\mathbf k)=g(t)W_D(-t,\mathbf k)u(\mathbf k)$. This is smooth and compactly supported in $(t,\mathbf k)$; its inverse spatial Fourier transform is Schwartz by repeated integration by parts. The definition in [F4] then gives $u_F=u$, and hence $P_\pm u_F=P_\pm u$. [F1, F4, F6, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 By steps 2.1 and 2.2 the particle and conjugate antiparticle test maps extend to unitaries on $\mathcal H_+$ and $\overline{\mathcal H_-}$. Their direct sum $T(\tilde g)$ is unitary. Define $U(\tilde g)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}T(\tilde g)^{\otimes_a n}$ on the antisymmetric Fock sectors. Each tensor power is unitary by its isometric action on elementary tensors and inverse tensor power; it commutes with the signed permutation average and therefore restricts to a unitary on the antisymmetric sector. The direct sum is unitary and fixes $\Omega$. On elementary wedge tensors the insertion/contraction formulas of [F5] give $U c^\dagger(h)U^{-1}=c^\dagger(Th)$ and $U c(h)U^{-1}=c(Th)$; density extends these identities to the finite-particle domain. Thus $U(\tilde g)\Psi(F)U(\tilde g)^{-1}=\Psi(\tau_{\tilde g}F)$. Direct substitution in the affine and spinor formulas gives $\tau_{\tilde g_2}\tau_{\tilde g_1}=\tau_{\tilde g_2\tilde g_1}$: the coordinate argument is $(\Lambda_2\Lambda_1)^{-1}(x-a_2-\Lambda_2a_1)$ and the matrix factor is $(S_2S_1)^{-\dagger}=S_2^{-\dagger}S_1^{-\dagger}$. By [F8] the Lorentz factors compose within $SO^+(1,3)$; by the definition of $\widetilde G$ its triples are closed under this product. Hence $T$ and its Fock lift $U$ obey the same product law and $U$ is a representation. [A1, F1, F4, F5, F8, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 The map $\tilde g\mapsto\tau_{\tilde g}F$ is continuous in Schwartz seminorms for each $F$, since it is composition with affine maps and finite matrices whose entries vary continuously. By the continuous test estimate of [F4], the one-particle representation is continuous on the dense test-generated subspaces of step 2.2; its operators have norm one, so approximation extends strong continuity to all one-particle vectors. On an elementary $n$-tensor, the difference of $T(g)^{\otimes n}$ and $T(g_0)^{\otimes n}$ is a sum of $n$ terms, each bounded by the norm of one factor difference times the norms of unchanged factors. It tends to zero as $g\to g_0$. Density and the unit norm bound extend this to each completed antisymmetric sector; finite-sector truncation then extends strong continuity to their direct sum. [F4, F5, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 By step 2.2 the ranges of $F\mapsto P_+u_F$ and $F\mapsto\overline{P_-u_F}$ are dense in $\mathcal H_+$ and $\overline{\mathcal H_-}$, respectively. Moreover, $\Psi(F)^\dagger\Omega=c^\dagger(P_+u_F)\Omega$ and $\Psi(F)\Omega=c^\dagger(\overline{P_-u_F})\Omega$, so their created one-particle components range densely over both summands. For any ordered list of $n$ such fields or adjoints, the all-creation term in their product on $\Omega$ is the wedge of their $n$ creation components. Expand the product into creation and annihilation terms and use the CAR to move every annihilator to the right: a term with a remaining annihilator kills $\Omega$, while each contraction leaves a product with at most $n-2$ creation factors. By induction, those lower-degree wedge vectors are in the polynomial orbit span, so subtracting them isolates the desired degree-$n$ wedge. The degree-zero base also lies in the orbit span: step 2.2 gives a test $F$ with $u_F\ne0$, and the CAR formula of [F4] gives $\{\Psi(F),\Psi(F)^\dagger\}=\|u_F\|^2I$, hence $I$ belongs to the generated algebra. Wedges of vectors from the dense one-particle ranges are dense in each antisymmetric sector by the Hilbert tensor completion, and finite-sector truncations are dense in Fock space. Hence $\Omega$ is cyclic for the global graded field algebra. [F1, F4, F5, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 For a pure translation, $\widehat{F(\cdot-a)}(t,\mathbf k)=\chi(-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf a)\widehat F(t-a^0,\mathbf k)$, so $u_{F(\cdot-a)}=W_D(a^0,\mathbf k)\chi(-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf a)u_F$. On $\mathcal H_+$ this is the phase $\chi(\omega a^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf a)$; after conjugation on $\overline{\mathcal H_-}$ it is $\chi(\omega a^0+\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf a)$. Thus the induced Fock translations are precisely those of [F7], whose joint spectrum is in the forward cone, whose zero-energy eigenspace is $\mathbb C\Omega$, and whose positive-$\mu$ gap is at least $\mu$. By [F9], $S_R(2\pi)=-I_4$ and $S_R(4\pi)=I_4$; hence a $2\pi$ rotation acts as $-I$ on each one-particle summand and $(-1)^n$ on sector $n$, while a $4\pi$ rotation is the identity. The first-quantized $h_D$ has eigenvalues $\pm\omega$, while the Fock translation time generator in [F7] multiplies both particle and antiparticle excitations by $+\omega$; their domains and Hilbert spaces differ. [F1, F2, F7, F9, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and the adopted Dirac branch of [[post-qft-free-field-model]] as specified by [[def-qft-free-dirac-model]]. For all Schwartz spinor tests $F,G$, the bounded smeared field $\Psi$ is antilinear in its test, satisfies
$$\{\Psi(F),\Psi(G)\}=0,\qquad \{\Psi(F),\Psi(G)^\dagger\}=\langle u_F,u_G\rangle I,$$
and solves the tested free Dirac equation. If $F$ and $G$ have compact spacelike-separated supports, the field-field and field-adjoint anticommutators vanish; consequently, finite even polynomials in the bounded smeared fields commute across spacelike-separated regions.

Let $\widetilde G_D$ be the translation and explicit spin-lift group defined in [[lem-qft-dirac-covariance-spectrum]]. Its strongly continuous unitary Fock representation $U$ satisfies
$$U(\widetilde g)\Psi(F)U(\widetilde g)^{-1}=\Psi(\tau_{\widetilde g}F),\qquad \tau_{\widetilde g}F(x)=(S^{-1})^\dagger F(\Lambda^{-1}(x-a)),$$
for $\widetilde g=(a,\Lambda,S)$. For the explicit spatial rotation lift, $S_R(2\pi)=-I_4$ and $S_R(4\pi)=I_4$; hence the $2\pi$ test pullback is $F\mapsto-F$ and $U_{2\pi}\Psi(F)U_{2\pi}^{-1}=-\Psi(F)$, while the $4\pi$ test pullback and field action are identities. The vacuum is invariant and cyclic for the global graded field algebra. On the $n$-particle sector, $U_{2\pi}=(-1)^n I$ and $U_{4\pi}=I$.

The joint spectrum of translations lies in the closed future cone and the vacuum is the unique zero-energy vector. For $\mu>0$, the nonvacuum spectrum has gap at least $\mu$ in inverse-length units, hence $m_{\mathrm{rest,SI}}c^2$ in SI energy units. If $K_D$ denotes the length-coordinate time-translation generator of [[lem-qft-dirac-covariance-spectrum]], the physical energy is $H_D^{\mathrm{SI}}=\hbar cK_D\ge0$ on the same domain. This Fock generator acts on a different Hilbert space from the first-quantized multiplier $h_D$, which has both signs of energy. These are conditional deductions in the adopted model, not empirical claims.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, $\mu\ge0$, the fixed $(-+++)$ and Fourier conventions, and the exact draft mathematical supplier interfaces stated below.

[A1] [[post-qft-free-field-model]] adopts the free Dirac CAR representation, species/statistics assignment and vacuum. This is a physical model assumption, not a derived theorem or empirical conclusion.

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]] defines the Countable Choice axiom assumed by the Fock and Dirac mathematical suppliers; no stronger choice principle is used.

[F1] [[def-qft-free-dirac-model]] fixes the selected $\mu\ge0$ branch, signature, length coordinates, one-particle branches and bounded smeared field; [[def-qft-framework-units]] specifies that inverse-length energy $\omega$ converts to SI energy $\hbar c\omega$.

[F2] [[lem-qft-free-dirac-car-locality]] assumes Countable Choice and the stated Dirac projections, Fock/CAR and Fourier suppliers. Its complete local draft proof establishes the continuous bounded smeared field, the two CAR identities and the tested Dirac equation.

[F3] The same [[lem-qft-free-dirac-car-locality]] proof establishes causal support of the anticommutator kernel and vanishing anticommutators for compact spacelike-separated tests; its statement derives graded locality. Its current mathematical supplier chain remains conditionally escalated on the scalar-causal and upstream QFT-MF01/MF02 inputs.

[F4] [[lem-qft-dirac-covariance-spectrum]] assumes Countable Choice and the exact Dirac, CAR, mass-shell, Lorentz and translation-spectrum suppliers. Its complete local draft proof establishes unitary spin-lift covariance, an invariant cyclic vacuum, the $2\pi$ and $4\pi$ actions, forward-cone spectrum, unique vacuum and positive-mass gap. Its current mathematical supplier chain remains conditionally escalated on the local CAR prerequisite and QFT-MF01/MF02 page inputs.

[F5] [[lem-qft-dirac-projection-matrices]] defines $S_R(\theta)=\cos(\theta/2)I_4-i\sin(\theta/2)\Sigma_{\mathbf n}$ for a unit rotation axis and proves it is the explicit spin lift used by [F4].

[F6] [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]] proves $\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x$ and $\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x$, with $\sin\pi=0$ and $\cos\pi=-1$; setting $x=\pi$ gives $\sin2\pi=0$ and $\cos2\pi=1$.

## Proof

1.1 Under [A1], the physical field and conventions are those fixed in [F1]. The mathematical construction [F2], with the Countable-Choice hypothesis [A2] and its Fock/CAR hypotheses, establishes the displayed smeared CAR relations and tested Dirac equation. Its causal-support conclusion [F3] gives vanishing anticommutators between fields supported in compact spacelike-separated regions; taking adjoints gives the adjoint-adjoint case. Thus every generator from one region anticommutes with every generator from the other. Reordering monomials of degrees $r$ and $s$ contributes $(-1)^{rs}$; for even $r,s$ this is $+1$, so bilinearity gives commutation of finite even polynomials. This deduction does not establish that the adopted model describes nature. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 The covariance and Fock-representation conclusions follow from [F4] under [A2] for the same $\mu$, metric, projection and CAR conventions. For a $2\pi$ spatial rotation, [F5] and [F6] give $S_R=\cos\pi I_4-i\sin\pi\Sigma_{\mathbf n}=-I_4$; the spacetime rotation is the identity, so the displayed pullback is $-F$ and antilinearity gives $U_{2\pi}\Psi(F)U_{2\pi}^{-1}=-\Psi(F)$. Substituting $x=\pi$ into the pi-shift identities in [F6] gives $\cos2\pi=1$ and $\sin2\pi=0$, hence $S_R(4\pi)=I_4$ and both pullback and field action are identities. The Fock action on each sector is supplied by [F4]. The same covariance supplier gives a strongly continuous unitary representation, invariant vacuum and cyclic global field algebra. [A2, F1, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1]

3.1 The covariance supplier in [F4] identifies its pure time-translation subgroup with the representation in its translation-spectrum supplier. That supplier defines the length-coordinate generator $H$ on the maximal multiplication domain by $U_{\mathrm{trans}}(a^0)=\chi(a^0H)$, where $\chi(s)=\cos s+i\sin s$; its joint spectrum is contained in the closed future cone, the vacuum is the zero-energy vector, and for $\mu>0$ the nonvacuum spectrum has gap at least $\mu$. Write $K_D:=H$ for the generator named in the Statement. Since $x^0=ct$, the SI time-evolution convention in [F1] gives
$$U_{\mathrm{evol}}(t)=U_{\mathrm{trans}}(-ct)=\chi(-ctK_D)=\exp(-ictK_D)=\exp(-itH_D^{\mathrm{SI}}/\hbar),$$
where $H_D^{\mathrm{SI}}=\hbar cK_D$ as in the Statement. Thus the forward-cone spectral result gives $K_D\ge0$ and hence $H_D^{\mathrm{SI}}\ge0$; for $\mu>0$ the SI gap is $\hbar c\mu=m_{\mathrm{rest,SI}}c^2$. The same supplier distinguishes this Fock generator from the two-signed first-quantized multiplier $h_D$, which acts on a different Hilbert space. [F1, F4, algebra] ∎

## Example

Define $\mathcal A_D^{\mathrm{even}}$ as the norm closure of finite linear combinations of the identity and even-degree products of $\Psi(F)$ and $\Psi(F)^\dagger$, for Schwartz spinor tests $F$. In the selected free Dirac model, let $U_{2\pi}$ implement a spatial rotation by $2\pi$ and let $U_{4\pi}$ implement a rotation by $4\pi$. On the $n$-particle sector of the adopted antisymmetric Fock decomposition, indexed by $n\in\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$, $U_{2\pi}$ acts as $(-1)^n$ times the identity; $U_{4\pi}=I$. Every finite even polynomial in bounded spacetime-smeared Dirac fields and their adjoints is invariant under conjugation by $U_{2\pi}$, and therefore so is $\mathcal A_D^{\mathrm{even}}$. This is an exact model calculation; it does not infer a general spin-statistics theorem.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The physical model and mathematical conventions of [[pthm-qft-dirac-free-properties]].

[F1] [[pthm-qft-dirac-free-properties]] proves that the $2\pi$ spin matrix is $-I_4$, the test pullback sends $F$ to $-F$, the field and its adjoint change sign, $U_{2\pi}$ acts on the $n$-particle sector as $(-1)^n$ for every $n\in\mathbb N_0$, and the $4\pi$ action is the identity.

[F2] [[pthm-qft-dirac-free-properties]] supplies the strongly continuous unitary Fock representation $U$ and its covariance action on the smeared field.

[F3] [[pthm-qft-dirac-free-properties]] states that the bounded smeared field $\Psi$ is antilinear in every Schwartz spinor test $F$.

## Verification

1.1 By [F1] and the covariance action in [F2], $U_{2\pi}\Psi(F)U_{2\pi}^{-1}=\Psi(-F)$. Antilinearity from [F3] gives $\Psi(-F)=-\Psi(F)$; taking adjoints gives the same sign for $\Psi(F)^\dagger$. The $4\pi$ action is the identity by [F1]. [F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 If $M=A_1\cdots A_r$ is a monomial whose factors are smeared fields or their adjoints, repeated use of step 1.1 and multiplicativity of unitary conjugation gives $U_{2\pi}MU_{2\pi}^{-1}=(-1)^rM$. Thus every even-degree monomial is fixed. Products of even-degree monomials and adjoints of even-degree monomials still have even degree, so finite linear combinations of them and the identity form a unital *-algebra; linearity fixes every such polynomial. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Conjugation by the unitary in [F2] is norm-continuous on bounded operators: $\|UOU^{-1}-UO'U^{-1}\|=\|O-O'\|$. Therefore every norm limit of finite even polynomials is also invariant. The conclusion concerns the algebra defined in the Example; it does not assert that pointwise field products exist. [F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $Q\sim N(0,C)$ be a centered scalar Gaussian with variance $C\ge0$.

[A1] The finite-dimensional normal-law suppliers explicitly assume the Axiom of Choice. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] A centered scalar normal with covariance $C$ is a one-dimensional instance of the multivariate normal law. [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]

[F2] The finite covariance Wick definition gives $:Q^2:_C=Q^2-C$. [[def-qft-finite-wick-normal-powers]]

[F3] The Gaussian pairing formula gives $\mathbb E[Q^2]=C$ and $\mathbb E[Q^4]=3C^2$. [[lem-qft-finite-gaussian-wick-moments]]

## Example

For a finite centered Gaussian coordinate, the expectation of the product of two Wick-subtracted quadratic powers is

$$\mathbb E\bigl[(:Q^2:_C)(:Q^2:_C)\bigr]=2C^2.$$

## Verification

**Proof technique:** expand the finite polynomials and apply the fourth-moment pairing formula.

**Given:** $C\ge0$ and [A1].

1.1 By [F2], $(:Q^2:_C)(:Q^2:_C)=(Q^2-C)^2=Q^4-2CQ^2+C^2$. [F2, algebra]

2.1 Taking expectations and substituting [F3] gives $3C^2-2C\cdot C+C^2=2C^2$. This also holds at the degenerate endpoint $C=0$, where the law is concentrated at zero. The Gaussian law is available under the stated Choice hypothesis [A1]. [A1, F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $U=\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, and $t\in\mathcal D'(U)$ have finite real scaling degree $\delta$. For every compact $K\subset U$ and every real $\omega>\delta$, there are an integer $m\ge0$ and $C<\infty$ such that

$$|\langle t_\rho,\psi\rangle|\le C\rho^{-\omega}p_m(\psi)\qquad(0<\rho\le1,\ \psi\in\mathcal D_K),$$

where $\mathcal D_K$ and $p_m(\psi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{x\in K}|\partial^\alpha\psi(x)|$ are the fixed-support test-function space and seminorms of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]]. The estimate is uniform over the entire moving-scale family, not merely over each fixed test separately.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $n\ge1$, $U=\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, $t\in\mathcal D'(U)$ with $\operatorname{sd}_0(t)=\delta\in\mathbb R$, a compact $K\subset U$, and $\omega>\delta$. Assume the Axiom of Choice.

[F1] [[def-qft-distribution-scaling-degree]]: $t_\rho(\psi)=\rho^{-n}t(\psi(\cdot/\rho))$, and $\delta$ is the infimum of the real exponents for which $\rho^\eta t_\rho\to0$ on every fixed test.

[F2] [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]]: $\mathcal D_K$ has increasing derivative seminorms $p_m$ and the compatible metric $d(\psi,\xi)=\sum_{m\ge0}2^{-m-1}\min(1,p_m(\psi-\xi))$.

[F3] [[lem-fixed-support-test-function-spaces-are-complete]]: this metric on $\mathcal D_K$ is complete and induces the seminorm topology, without a choice axiom.

[F4] [[def-dependent-choice]]: DC supplies an $\mathbb N$-indexed chain for any serial relation and prescribed initial point.

[F5] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC selects an element from every set-indexed family of nonempty sets.

[F6] [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]: in ZF, AC implies DC.

[F7] [[thm-baire-category-for-complete-metric-spaces]]: under DC, a nonempty complete metric space cannot be a countable union of closed sets with empty interior.

[F8] [[def-countable-choice]]: AC$_\omega$ selects a point from each sequence of nonempty sets.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is assumed.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the statement.

1.1 Let $X=\mathcal D_K$ with the metric of [F2]. It is nonempty because it contains $0$, and it is complete by [F3]. AC supplies DC by [F4]–[F6], so the Baire theorem [F7] applies. The proof of [F7] also chooses centers for its recursively constructed balls; that countable family of nonempty balls is covered by AC$_\omega$ from [F6] and [F8]. [given, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, A1]

1.2 For fixed $\psi\in X$, set $L_\rho(\psi)=\rho^\omega\langle t_\rho,\psi\rangle$. The exponents $\eta$ for which $\rho^\eta t_\rho(\psi)\to0$ for every fixed test form an upward-closed set: if the limit holds at $\eta$, then for $\omega>\eta$ multiply by $\rho^{\omega-\eta}\le1$. Since its infimum is $\delta<\omega$, some such $\eta$ is below $\omega$, and consequently $L_\rho(\psi)\to0$ as $\rho\downarrow0$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 On any compact scale interval $[\epsilon,1]$ with $\epsilon>0$, the tests $\psi(\cdot/\rho)$ have support in one compact subset of $U$ and vary continuously in every derivative seminorm by the chain rule. Continuity of the distribution $t$ therefore makes $\rho\mapsto L_\rho(\psi)$ continuous there. Together with step 1.2 this proves $\sup_{0<\rho\le1}|L_\rho(\psi)|<\infty$ for every $\psi\in X$. [F1, F2, step 1.2]

3.1 For each positive integer $N$, let $E_N=\{\psi\in X:\sup_{0<\rho\le1}|L_\rho(\psi)|\le N\}$. Each $E_N$ is closed because every $L_\rho$ is a continuous linear functional on $X$. Step 2.1 gives $X=\bigcup_{N\ge1}E_N$. By [F7], some $E_N$ has nonempty interior. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F7]

4.1 The topology of $X$ is generated by the increasing seminorms in [F2], so for some $\psi_0\in E_N$, $m\ge0$, and $\varepsilon>0$, the set $\psi_0+\{\zeta:p_m(\zeta)<\varepsilon\}$ lies in $E_N$. For every such $\zeta$, subtracting the two bounds for $\psi_0+\zeta$ and $\psi_0$ gives $|L_\rho(\zeta)|\le2N$ for all $\rho$. If $p_m(\psi)>0$, apply this to $\zeta=\varepsilon\psi/(2p_m(\psi))$; if $p_m(\psi)=0$, then $p_0(\psi)=0$ and hence $\psi=0$. Thus $|L_\rho(\psi)|\le(4N/\varepsilon)p_m(\psi)$ for every $\psi$ and every $0<\rho\le1$. Replacing $L_\rho$ by its definition proves the claimed uniform order estimate. [F2, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $U=\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, and let $t\in\mathcal D'(U)$ have finite real scaling degree $\delta=\operatorname{sd}_0(t)$. Then there exists $T\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ such that $T|_U=t$ and $\operatorname{sd}_0(T)=\delta$. The result applies to arbitrary distributions with finite real scaling degree; it assumes no smooth kernel or pointwise product representation.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $n\ge1$, $t\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\})$ with finite real scaling degree $\delta$, and the Axiom of Choice.

[F1] [[def-qft-distribution-scaling-degree]]: $t_\rho(\varphi)=\rho^{-n}t(\varphi(\cdot/\rho))$; convergence and scaling degree are tested on each fixed test function.

[F2] [[lem-qft-test-frechet-uniform-scaling-order]]: under AC, every fixed compact annular test support has a finite derivative order and uniform bound for the family $\rho^\omega t_\rho$, for each $\omega>\delta$.

[F3] [[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]]: a smooth compactly supported cutoff equal to one near the origin exists in ZF.

[F4] [[thm-multivariable-taylor-formula-with-lagrange-remainder]]: for smooth tests, subtracting the Taylor polynomial through order $k$ leaves a remainder of order $|x|^{k+1}$ locally; applying the theorem to derivatives gives the corresponding differentiated estimates.

[F5] [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]: $\mathcal D(V)=C_c^\infty(V;\mathbb C)$, with actual smooth compactly supported functions as tests.

[F6] [[def-test-function-topology]]: $\mathcal D(V)$ has the locally convex LF topology determined by its fixed-support test spaces; continuity of a linear functional is checked on each fixed-support stage.

[F7] [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]: differentiation, multiplication by a fixed smooth function, and pullback by a fixed smooth diffeomorphism act continuously on the corresponding test-function spaces.

[F8] [[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]: $\langle\partial^\alpha\delta_0,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\partial^\alpha\varphi(0)$; the jet evaluations used below are continuous.

[A1] Assume AC; it is used through the Baire estimate [F2], whose proof invokes DC.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the statement.

1.1 Choose $\chi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$ equal to one near $0$ by [F3], and put $f(x)=\chi(x)-\chi(2x)$. Its support $K$ is compact and avoids $0$, so choose $0<a<b<\infty$ with $K\subset\{x:a\le|x|\le b\}$. If $\delta<n$, set $k=-1$ and $W\varphi=\varphi$. If $\delta\ge n$, let $k$ be the integer with $k\le\delta-n<k+1$, put $P_k\varphi(x)=\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}x^\alpha\partial^\alpha\varphi(0)/\alpha!$, and define $W\varphi=\varphi-\chi P_k\varphi$. [given, F3, F4, F5, A1]

2.1 For $\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$ define $$T(\varphi):=\langle t,(1-\chi)W\varphi\rangle+\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\langle t,f(2^j\cdot)W\varphi\rangle.$$ Each pairing is with a test supported in $U$: the first factor vanishes near $0$, and $f(2^j\cdot)$ is supported in $2^{-j}K$. [F1, F3, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Choose $\omega$ with $\delta<\omega<n+k+1$; this interval is nonempty by the choice of $k$. Put $\lambda=2^{-j}$. By the dilation convention [F1], $$\langle t,f(\cdot/\lambda)W\varphi\rangle=\lambda^n\langle t_\lambda,f\,W\varphi(\lambda\cdot)\rangle.$$ The uniform estimate [F2] bounds this by $C\lambda^{n-\omega}p_m(f\,W\varphi(\lambda\cdot))$ for fixed $m,C$. When $k\ge0$ and $\lambda$ is small enough that $\chi=1$ on $\lambda K$, [F4] gives $p_m(f\,W\varphi(\lambda\cdot))\le C_\varphi\lambda^{k+1}$. Indeed, after each derivative of order $q\le m$, the Taylor remainder contributes order $\lambda^{k+1-q}$ if $q\le k$, and the chain-rule factor contributes $\lambda^q$; if $q>k$, the factor $\lambda^q$ is already at most $\lambda^{k+1}$ for $\lambda\le1$. The product rule with the fixed smooth $f$ preserves this bound. When $k=-1$, the same seminorm is bounded by $C_\varphi$. Thus the tail is bounded by a convergent geometric series with exponent $n+k+1-\omega>0$ (or $n-\omega>0$ when $k=-1$). The series in step 2.1 is absolutely convergent. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For tests supported in any fixed compact $C\subset\mathbb R^n$, the first term of step 2.1 is a continuous functional: its input is supported in a fixed compact subset of $U$, and the cutoff, multiplication, and finite jet maps are continuous by [F5]–[F8]. The geometric bound of step 3.1 controls the small-scale annular tail by one finite derivative seminorm on a compact containing $C$ and $0$; the finitely many larger scales are continuous by [F1] and [F7]. Hence $T$ is continuous on every fixed-support test space and is a distribution by [F6]. [F1, F5, F6, F7, F8, step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 If $\varphi$ is supported away from $0$, all its jets at $0$ vanish, so $W\varphi=\varphi$. The partial sums telescope: $$\sum_{j=0}^{N}f(2^j x)=\chi(x)-\chi(2^{N+1}x).$$ For sufficiently large $N$, $\chi(2^{N+1}x)=0$ on the support of $\varphi$. Adding the first term of step 2.1 then gives $T(\varphi)=\langle t,\varphi\rangle$. Thus $T|_U=t$. [F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra]

5.2 Fix $\Omega>\delta$ and choose $\omega$ with $\delta<\omega<\min(\Omega,n+k+1)$. Write $\varphi_\rho(x)=\rho^{-n}\varphi(x/\rho)$, so $T_\rho(\varphi)=T(\varphi_\rho)$. Choose $R$ with $\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subset B(0,R)$ and $C>R/a$, where $a$ is from step 1.1. Choose $\lambda_0>0$ so $\chi=1$ on $\lambda K$ for $0<\lambda\le\lambda_0$, and take $\rho$ small enough that $C\rho\le\lambda_0$ and $\operatorname{supp}\varphi_\rho$ lies where $\chi=1$. For a shell $\lambda K$ with $\lambda>C\rho$, its inner radius is at least $a\lambda>R\rho$, so $\varphi_\rho$ vanishes there. If $k=-1$, the first term in step 2.1 and all such coarse-shell terms are therefore zero. On the remaining shells $\lambda\le C\rho$, the chain rule and boundedness of $\lambda/\rho$ give $p_m(f\varphi_\rho(\lambda\cdot))\le C_\varphi\rho^{-n}$; their dyadic sum is $O(\rho^{-\omega})$ because $n-\omega>0$. If $k\ge0$, on each fine shell $\lambda\le C\rho$ the cutoff is one. For every derivative order $q\le m$, Taylor's formula for $\varphi-P_k\varphi$ when $q\le k$, and the chain-rule factor $(\lambda/\rho)^q$ when $q>k$, give $p_m(f\,W\varphi_\rho(\lambda\cdot))\le C_\varphi\rho^{-n-k-1}\lambda^{k+1}$; the fixed upper bound $\lambda/\rho\le C$ absorbs the finitely many higher derivative orders. Hence these shells contribute at most $$C_\varphi\rho^{-n-k-1}\sum_{\substack{\lambda=2^{-j},\ j\ge0\\\lambda\le C\rho}}\lambda^{n+k+1-\omega}=O(\rho^{-\omega}),$$ because $n+k+1-\omega>0$ and the dyadic sum is bounded by a constant times $\rho^{n+k+1-\omega}$. On the intermediate coarse shells $C\rho<\lambda\le\lambda_0$, only the subtracted Taylor polynomial remains. Its degree-$j$ term, $0\le j\le k$, contributes at most $C_\varphi\rho^{-n-j}\lambda^{n+j-\omega}$. Since $\omega>\delta\ge n+k\ge n+j$, the exponent $n+j-\omega$ is negative; summing dyadically from the smallest such $\lambda\asymp\rho$ up to $\lambda_0$ gives $O(\rho^{-\omega})$. For the finitely many outer shells $\lambda_0<\lambda\le1$ and the first term of step 2.1, continuity of $t$ on their fixed compact supports bounds the jet contributions by $O(\rho^{-n-k})=O(\rho^{-\omega})$, since $\omega>\delta\ge n+k$. Thus in both the fine and coarse regions $|T_\rho(\varphi)|\le C_\varphi\rho^{-\omega}$ for small $\rho$. Therefore $|T_\rho(\varphi)|\le C_\varphi\rho^{-\omega}$ for small $\rho$ in both cases, so $\rho^\Omega T_\rho(\varphi)\to0$. This proves $\operatorname{sd}_0(T)\le\delta$. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 If an exponent $\Omega<\delta$ made $\rho^\Omega T_\rho\to0$, restricting to tests supported in $U$ and using step 5.1 would give $\rho^\Omega t_\rho\to0$, contrary to $\operatorname{sd}_0(t)=\delta$. Hence $\operatorname{sd}_0(T)\ge\delta$. Together with step 5.2, $\operatorname{sd}_0(T)=\delta$. [F1, step 5.1, step 5.2] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $t\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\})$ have finite real scaling degree $\delta$, and let $\mathcal E_\delta(t)$ be the set of its extensions in $\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ having scaling degree exactly $\delta$. This set is nonempty by [[thm-qft-finite-scaling-degree-extension]]. If $\delta<n$, then $\mathcal E_\delta(t)$ has exactly one member. If $\delta\ge n$, let $k$ be the unique nonnegative integer with $k\le\delta-n<k+1$ (the floor of $\delta-n$). Then, for any $T_0\in\mathcal E_\delta(t)$,

$$\mathcal E_\delta(t)=T_0+\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{\partial^\alpha\delta_0:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$

Here a **point-local counterterm** means a distribution whose support, as defined in [[def-support-of-a-distribution]], is contained in $\{0\}$. Thus the same-degree freedom is finite dimensional, with precisely the displayed delta derivatives as its basis; at the threshold $\delta=n$, only a multiple of $\delta_0$ is allowed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $n\ge1$, $t\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\})$ with finite real scaling degree $\delta$, and the Axiom of Choice.

[F1] [[def-qft-distribution-scaling-degree]]: the distribution dilation is $T_\rho(\varphi)=\rho^{-n}T(\varphi(\cdot/\rho))$, and scaling degree is defined by convergence of $\rho^\omega T_\rho$.

[F2] [[thm-qft-finite-scaling-degree-extension]]: under AC, every punctured distribution with finite real scaling degree $\delta$ has at least one extension of exactly that degree.

[F3] [[thm-distributions-supported-at-one-point]]: a distribution supported in $\{0\}$ is a unique finite sum $\sum_\alpha c_\alpha\partial^\alpha\delta_0$.

[F4] [[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]: $\langle\partial^\alpha\delta_0,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\partial^\alpha\varphi(0)$.

[F5] [[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]]: a smooth compact cutoff equal to one near $\{0\}$ exists in $\mathbb R^n$.

[F6] [[def-support-of-a-distribution]]: the support is the complement of the largest open set where the distribution vanishes; agreement on tests away from $0$ makes the difference supported at $\{0\}$.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is assumed, as required by [F2].

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the statement.

1.1 By [F2], choose $T_0\in\mathcal E_\delta(t)$. For any $T\in\mathcal E_\delta(t)$ the difference $S=T-T_0$ vanishes on every test supported away from $0$, so $\operatorname{supp}S\subseteq\{0\}$ by [F6]. By [F3], $S=\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}c_\alpha\partial^\alpha\delta_0$ for some finite $m$. [given, F2, F3, F6, A1]

2.1 For $S\ne0$, let $m$ be the largest order with a nonzero coefficient, and choose $\alpha$ of order $m$ with $c_\alpha\ne0$. Choose $\eta\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$ equal to one near $0$ by [F5], and test with $\psi_\alpha(x)=\eta(x)x^\alpha/\alpha!$. The product rule gives $\partial^\beta\psi_\alpha(0)=0$ for all $|\beta|\le m$ except $\beta=\alpha$, where it equals $1$. Consequently $$\langle S_\rho,\psi_\alpha\rangle=(-1)^m c_\alpha\rho^{-n-m}.$$ For every test $\varphi$, [F4] likewise gives $\langle S_\rho,\varphi\rangle=\sum_\beta c_\beta(-1)^{|\beta|}\rho^{-n-|\beta|}\partial^\beta\varphi(0)$. The finite sum tends to zero after multiplication by $\rho^\omega$ for every $\omega>n+m$, while the chosen test prevents convergence to zero for $\omega<n+m$. Hence $\operatorname{sd}_0(S)=n+m$. [F1, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Since $T$ and $T_0$ both have degree $\delta$, for every $\omega>\delta$ both $\rho^\omega T_\rho$ and $\rho^\omega(T_0)_\rho$ tend to zero. Thus $\operatorname{sd}_0(S)\le\delta$. Step 2.1 implies that every nonzero coefficient in $S$ has order at most $\lfloor\delta-n\rfloor$; if $\delta<n$, no nonzero $S$ is possible. [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Conversely, let $S$ be any finite sum of $\partial^\alpha\delta_0$ with $|\alpha|\le k$ when $\delta\ge n$. Step 2.1 gives $\operatorname{sd}_0(S)\le n+k\le\delta$, and $T_0+S$ still restricts to $t$. Hence $\operatorname{sd}_0(T_0+S)\le\delta$. Restriction to tests supported in $\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$ gives $\operatorname{sd}_0(T_0+S)\ge\operatorname{sd}_0(t)=\delta$, so equality holds. Uniqueness of the coefficients in [F3] identifies the displayed finite-dimensional affine space. For $\delta=n$, $k=0$, giving only $c\delta_0$. [F1, F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. On $\mathbb R^4\setminus\{0\}$ let $u(x)=1/(16\pi^4|x|^4)$, equivalently the square of the displayed Euclidean kernel $C_0(x)=1/(4\pi^2|x|^2)$; interpret $u$ as its regular distribution there. Choose $\chi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^4)$ equal to one near $0$. For $\mu>0$ define

$$T_\mu(\varphi):=\int_{\mathbb R^4\setminus\{0\}}\frac{\varphi(x)-\chi(\mu x)\varphi(0)}{16\pi^4|x|^4}\,d^4x.$$

Then $T_\mu$ is a distribution extending $u$, has scaling degree $4$, and for every $\mu,\nu>0$,

$$T_\mu-T_\nu=\frac{1}{8\pi^2}\log(\mu/\nu)\,\delta_0.$$

In particular, no extension of $u$ with scaling degree $4$ is exactly homogeneous, where exact homogeneity means $\rho^4T_\rho=T$ for every $\rho>0$. Coordinates use one fixed Euclidean unit; if units are assigned, $\mu$ and $\nu$ have reciprocal coordinate units, so the logarithm's ratio is dimensionless. This is a Euclidean distribution identity and does not identify a measured coupling or physical beta function.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Euclidean space $\mathbb R^4$, the regular distribution induced by $u(x)=1/(16\pi^4|x|^4)$ on the punctured domain, a smooth compact cutoff $\chi=1$ near $0$, and $\mu,\nu>0$. Assume the Axiom of Choice.

[F1] [[def-qft-distribution-scaling-degree]]: $T_\rho(\varphi)=\rho^{-4}T(\varphi(\cdot/\rho))$; $\operatorname{sd}_0(T)$ is determined by the limits $\rho^\omega T_\rho$.

[F2] [[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]]: there is a real smooth compact cutoff equal to one near $0$.

[F3] [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]]: a locally integrable function acts by the bilinear pairing $\varphi\mapsto\int u\varphi$.

[F4] [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]: under AC$_\omega$, this regular functional is a distribution.

[F5] [[def-countable-choice]]: AC$_\omega$ chooses from every sequence of nonempty sets.

[F6] [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]: in ZF, AC implies both DC and AC$_\omega$.

[F7] [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]] defines the finite-dimensional angular measure $\sigma_3$; [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]] gives the polar integral formula under AC$_\omega$.

[F8] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: nonnegative product-measurable functions integrate by iterated integrals on sigma-finite product spaces.

[F9] [[thm-gaussian-integral]]: $\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-s^2}\,ds=\sqrt\pi$.

[F10] [[thm-qft-finite-scaling-degree-extension]]: under AC, the punctured distribution has at least one extension with its finite scaling degree.

[F11] [[prop-qft-local-counterterm-jet-classification]]: same-degree extensions differ by precisely the permitted finite delta jets; at $\delta=n$ the difference is a multiple of $\delta_0$.

[F12] [[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]: $\langle\delta_0,\varphi\rangle=\varphi(0)$ and $\langle\partial^\alpha\delta_0,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\partial^\alpha\varphi(0)$.

[F13] [[def-test-function-topology]]: continuity on $\mathcal D(\mathbb R^4)$ is determined by continuity on each fixed-support test space.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is assumed. It supplies AC$_\omega$ for [F4] and [F7] by [F6], and DC for the scaling-degree extension theorem [F10].

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the statement.

1.1 The function $u$ is smooth, hence locally integrable, on $U=\mathbb R^4\setminus\{0\}$. By [F3]–[F6] it defines a distribution $t\in\mathcal D'(U)$; direct dilation gives $t_\rho=\rho^{-4}t$, so $\operatorname{sd}_0(t)=4$. [given, F1, F3, F4, F5, F6, A1, algebra]

1.2 Let $\sigma_3$ be the polar surface measure on $S^3$. By [F7]–[F9] and Tonelli, $$\pi^2=\int_{\mathbb R^4}e^{-|x|^2}\,d^4x=\sigma_3(S^3)\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2}r^3\,dr=\frac{\sigma_3(S^3)}2.$$ The last integral is $1/2$ by $s=r^2$ and integration by parts. Therefore $\sigma_3(S^3)=2\pi^2$. [F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, algebra]

2.1 Near $0$, $\chi(\mu x)=1$ and $|\varphi(x)-\varphi(0)|\le |x|\sup_{B}|\nabla\varphi|$ on a compact ball $B$ containing $0$ and the fixed test support. Thus the integrand is bounded by a fixed seminorm times $|x|^{-3}$ there, which is integrable in four dimensions. Away from $0$ its support is contained in the compact union of $\operatorname{supp}\varphi$ and $\mu^{-1}\operatorname{supp}\chi$, and $|x|^{-4}$ is bounded on that support; the remaining pairing is bounded by a fixed zeroth-order seminorm, including the evaluation $|\varphi(0)|$. These bounds hold uniformly on each fixed-support test space, so $T_\mu$ is continuous there and hence a distribution by [F13]. If $\varphi$ is supported away from $0$, then $\varphi(0)=0$, so $T_\mu(\varphi)=t(\varphi)$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F13, step 1.1]

2.2 Subtracting the two definitions gives $$T_\mu(\varphi)-T_\nu(\varphi)=-\frac{\varphi(0)}{16\pi^4}\int_{\mathbb R^4\setminus\{0\}}\frac{\chi(\mu x)-\chi(\nu x)}{|x|^4}\,d^4x.$$ The difference vanishes on a fixed neighborhood of $0$ and outside a fixed compact set, so it is absolutely integrable. Apply [F7] separately to its positive and negative parts; the integral is $\int_{S^3}\int_0^\infty[\chi(\mu r\omega)-\chi(\nu r\omega)]\,dr/r\,d\sigma_3(\omega)$. For $\mu$ in a compact interval $[\mu_0,\mu_1]\subset(0,\infty)$ choose $0<a<b$ so every first or second derivative of $\chi$ vanishes unless $a\le|y|\le b$. Writing $s=\log\mu$ and $g(s,r,\omega)=\chi(e^s r\omega)$, the first and second $s$-derivatives vanish unless $a/\mu_1\le r\le b/\mu_0$. On this annulus, $|\partial_s^2g|\le b\|\nabla\chi\|_\infty+b^2\|D^2\chi\|_\infty=:M$, by the chain rule; these suprema are finite because $\chi$ is smooth and compactly supported. For $s$ in a smaller compact interval and $h$ sufficiently small, the one-variable Taylor estimate gives $|(g(s+h,r,\omega)-g(s,r,\omega))/h-\partial_sg(s,r,\omega)|\le M|h|/2$ uniformly in $r,\omega$. The annulus has finite $dr/r$ measure and $S^3$ has finite measure by step 1.2, so integrating this uniform error proves differentiation under the polar integral. For each $\omega$, $$\int_0^\infty\frac{\partial}{\partial\log\mu}\chi(\mu r\omega)\,\frac{dr}{r} =\int_0^\infty\nabla\chi(s\omega)\cdot\omega\,ds =\chi(\infty\omega)-\chi(0)=-1,$$ where $s=\mu r$, $\chi=1$ near $0$, and $\chi$ is compactly supported. Since the difference integral vanishes at $\mu=\nu$, its value is $-\sigma_3(S^3)\log(\mu/\nu)$. With step 1.2 this proves the displayed formula for $T_\mu-T_\nu$. [F2, F7, F12, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Changing variables in the defining integral and using $u(\rho x)=\rho^{-4}u(x)$ gives $\rho^4(T_\mu)_\rho=T_{\rho\mu}$. Step 2.2 with $(\rho\mu,\mu)$ then gives $$\rho^4(T_\mu)_\rho=T_\mu+\frac{1}{8\pi^2}\log\rho\,\delta_0.$$ For every $\Omega>4$, multiplication by $\rho^{\Omega-4}$ makes the right side tend to zero as $\rho\downarrow0$, so $\operatorname{sd}_0(T_\mu)\le4$. Restriction to $U$ and step 1.1 give the reverse inequality, hence $\operatorname{sd}_0(T_\mu)=4$. [F1, F12, step 1.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 The exact-degree extension family is nonempty by [F10], and [F11] says every member differs from $T_\mu$ by $c\delta_0$. Since $\rho^4(\delta_0)_\rho=\delta_0$, the scaling identity of step 3.1 yields $\rho^4(T_\mu+c\delta_0)_\rho=T_\mu+c\delta_0+(8\pi^2)^{-1}\log\rho\,\delta_0$, which is not constant in $\rho$. ## Statement

Let $D\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}$ and let $\Gamma$ be a finite quartic graph in the sense of [[def-qft-quartic-graph-power-counting]]. With $V$ vertices, $I$ internal edges, $E$ external half-edges, and loop count $L$, the incidence and loop-count identities are $4V=2I+E$ and $L=I-V+1$. Its superficial degree under the stated Euclidean scalar power-counting convention is $\omega_D(\Gamma)=DL-2I=D+(D-4)V-\frac{D-2}{2}E$. In $D=4$ this reduces to $\omega_4(\Gamma)=4-E$. A zero value is a logarithmic **superficial** degree by the convention in the definition; these identities do not assert convergence or divergence of an actual graph integral.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $D\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}$ and a finite connected multigraph $\Gamma$ with $V\ge1$ four-slot vertices, $I$ internal edges, and $E$ external half-edges, using degree $D$ per loop integration and degree $-2$ per internal scalar propagator.

[F1] [[def-qft-quartic-graph-power-counting]]: the internal-edge ends and the attached external half-edges are in bijection with the four incidence slots at each vertex; $L:=I-V+1$ is the cycle rank; one formal loop integration contributes degree $D$, each internal scalar propagator contributes degree $-2$, and $\omega_D(\Gamma):=DL-2I$. The value $\omega_D=0$ is called logarithmic superficial degree and is only formal graph bookkeeping.

## Proof

**Given:** The graph and power-counting data in [F1].

1.1 Counting the four slots at every vertex gives $4V$ slots. Each of the $I$ internal edges occupies two slots, including a self-loop, and each of the $E$ external half-edges occupies one. Hence $4V=2I+E$. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 Start with one vertex and repeatedly add an internal edge from the reached vertices to a vertex not yet reached. Connectedness provides such an edge until all $V$ vertices are reached. Each added edge introduces one new vertex, so the selected edges form a spanning tree with $V-1$ edges; for $V=1$ it is empty. Exactly $I-(V-1)=I-V+1=L$ internal edges lie outside this tree, including any unselected loops or parallel edges, so the cycle rank in [F1] is nonnegative and counts the non-tree internal edges. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 By [F1], $\omega_D=DL-2I$. Substitute $L=I-V+1$ from step 1.2 to obtain $\omega_D=(D-2)I-DV+D$. From step 1.1, $I=2V-E/2$, so $\omega_D=(D-2)(2V-E/2)-DV+D=D+(D-4)V-\frac{D-2}{2}E$. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Setting $D=4$ in step 2.1 gives $\omega_4=4-E$. The defining convention in [F1] calls its zero value logarithmic superficial degree; it makes no claim about an actual integral's convergence or divergence. [F1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. In the selected model of
[[post-qft-free-field-model]], let $H_\mu$ be the scalar one-particle Hilbert
space and let $\mathcal K=\mathcal H_+\oplus\overline{\mathcal H_-}$ be the
Dirac particle/antiparticle one-particle space. Let $\Omega_s$ and $\Omega_D$
be their zero-particle Fock vectors. The assignments of $H_\mu$ to bosonic
Fock space and $\mathcal K$ to CAR Fock space are the physical assumptions
of that postulate.

For every unit scalar wave-packet mode $h\in H_\mu$, define
$$|n\rangle_h=\frac{(a^\dagger(h))^n}{\sqrt{n!}}\Omega_s,\qquad n\ge0.$$
These vectors are normalized and mutually orthogonal, belong to the
finite-particle domain, and
$$a(h)|n\rangle_h=\sqrt n\,|n-1\rangle_h,\qquad a^\dagger(h)|n\rangle_h=\sqrt{n+1}\,|n+1\rangle_h,$$
where $a(h)|0\rangle_h=0$. The maximal operator domains supplied by
[[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]] are
$$D(a(h))=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n)\in\mathcal F_s(H_\mu):\sum_{n\ge1}\|a_n(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad D(a^\dagger(h))=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n)\in\mathcal F_s(H_\mu):\sum_{n\ge0}\|a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
Define the one-mode number operator as the composition
$$N_h:=a^\dagger(h)a(h),\qquad D(N_h):=\{\Psi\in D(a(h)):a(h)\Psi\in D(a^\dagger(h))\},\qquad N_h\Psi:=a^\dagger(h)(a(h)\Psi).$$
The displayed finite-particle vectors $|n\rangle_h$ belong to $D(N_h)$ and
satisfy $N_h|n\rangle_h=n|n\rangle_h$.

For every unit Dirac particle mode $u\in\mathcal H_+$ or antiparticle mode
$u\in\overline{\mathcal H_-}$, regarded as a vector of $\mathcal K$, the
bounded operator $N_u=c^\dagger(u)c(u)$ is an orthogonal projection. The
one-mode subspace generated by $u$ is the closed span of
$\{(c^\dagger(u))^n\Omega_D:n\ge0\}$. It is spanned by $\Omega_D$ and
$c^\dagger(u)\Omega_D$; the latter is normalized and
$c^\dagger(u)^2=0$. Thus a single Dirac CAR mode has occupation $0$ or $1$.
All statements are conditional on the adopted representations and
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. They do not derive which statistics nature assigns to
all fields and do not assert an experimental observation.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The physical species assignments in [A1], Countable Choice in
[A2], and the mathematical Fock operator construction in [F1].

[A1] [[post-qft-free-field-model]] adopts the real scalar bosonic
symmetric-Fock model and the Dirac particle/antiparticle CAR-Fock model. This
is a physical model assumption, not a universal statistics theorem.

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]] states $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$: every sequence of
nonempty sets has a choice function. The Fock supplier assumes this principle,
which is carried into this consumer.

[F1] [[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]] assumes $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and a separable
complex Hilbert space. It constructs the symmetric and antisymmetric Fock
spaces and proves that $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is dense; the bosonic operators
are mutual adjoints on their displayed domains and on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ satisfy
$[a(h),a^\dagger(k)]=\langle h,k\rangle_2 I$, while the fermionic operators
are bounded on the whole Fock space and satisfy
$\{c(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=\langle h,k\rangle_2 I$ and
$\{c^\dagger(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=0$.

[F2] [[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]] gives the exact bosonic maximal domains displayed in the Statement.

[F3] [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]] defines each Fock vacuum as
$\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$, defines creation and annihilation by sector
insertion and contraction, and states $a(h)\Omega=c(h)\Omega=0$.

## Proof

**Given:** [A1], [A2], and [F1]–[F3].

1.1 Fix a unit $h\in H_\mu$ and put $v_n=(a^\dagger(h))^n\Omega_s$. The
vacuum relation is $a(h)\Omega_s=0$ and the CCR give
$a(h)a^\dagger(h)=a^\dagger(h)a(h)+I$. The base case is
$a(h)v_1=\Omega_s$. If $a(h)v_n=nv_{n-1}$, then
$a(h)v_{n+1}=a(h)a^\dagger(h)v_n
=a^\dagger(h)a(h)v_n+v_n
=n a^\dagger(h)v_{n-1}+v_n=(n+1)v_n$.
Thus $a(h)v_n=nv_{n-1}$ for every $n\ge1$. [given, A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 Fix a unit $u\in\mathcal K$. By [F1],
$c(u)c^\dagger(u)+c^\dagger(u)c(u)=I$ and $c^\dagger(u)^2=0$. On
finite-particle vectors, the insertion and contraction formulas of [F3] give
$\langle c^\dagger(u)\xi,\eta\rangle_2=
\langle\xi,c(u)\eta\rangle_2$: the antisymmetric projection can be removed
against $\eta$, after which the tensor pairing contracts the inserted $u$
with the first factor. Since both operators are bounded by [F1] and
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is dense by [F1], this identity extends to the whole
Fock space and gives $c^\dagger(u)=c(u)^*$. Also $c(u)\Omega_D=0$ by [F3].
Hence
$\|c^\dagger(u)\Omega_D\|^2
=\langle\Omega_D,c(u)c^\dagger(u)\Omega_D\rangle_2
=\langle\Omega_D,(I-c^\dagger(u)c(u))\Omega_D\rangle_2=1$.
A second creation vanishes. Since vacuum and one-particle sectors are
orthogonal, the cyclic subspace generated by $u$ is exactly
$\operatorname{span}\{\Omega_D,c^\dagger(u)\Omega_D\}$. Moreover,
$N_u^*=N_u$ and
$N_u^2=c^\dagger(u)(I-c^\dagger(u)c(u))c(u)=N_u$ because
$c^\dagger(u)^2=0$. Thus $N_u$ is a projection, so its only possible
eigenvalues are $0$ and $1$; it acts as $0$ on $\Omega_D$ and as $1$ on
$c^\dagger(u)\Omega_D$. [A1, A2, F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 Since $a^\dagger(h)$ and $a(h)$ are mutual adjoints on the finite-sector
vectors, $\|v_{n+1}\|^2=\langle v_n,a(h)a^\dagger(h)v_n\rangle_2
=(n+1)\|v_n\|^2$. Starting from $\|v_0\|=1$ gives $\|v_n\|^2=n!$.
The vectors $v_n$ lie in distinct Fock sectors and are orthogonal.
Consequently the displayed $|n\rangle_h$ are orthonormal, and dividing
$a(h)v_n=n v_{n-1}$ by the factorial normalizations gives
$a(h)|n\rangle_h=\sqrt n|n-1\rangle_h$. The creation formula gives
$a^\dagger(h)|n\rangle_h=\sqrt{n+1}|n+1\rangle_h$. The exact domains [F2]
show that every finite-particle vector lies in both $D(a(h))$ and
$D(a^\dagger(h))$, since each defining sum then has only finitely many finite
sector terms. For $n\ge1$, $a(h)|n\rangle_h=\sqrt n|n-1\rangle_h$ is finite-particle,
so $|n\rangle_h\in D(a(h))$ and $a(h)|n\rangle_h\in D(a^\dagger(h))$; hence
$|n\rangle_h\in D(N_h)$ and
$N_h|n\rangle_h=a^\dagger(h)(\sqrt n|n-1\rangle_h)=n|n\rangle_h$.
For $n=0$, $a(h)|0\rangle_h=0\in D(a^\dagger(h))$, so $|0\rangle_h\in D(N_h)$
and $N_h|0\rangle_h=0$. [A2, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The scalar ladder and Dirac one-mode exclusion above follow only after
the species-to-Fock assignments in [A1] are made. The argument uses the
specified representations and proves no relation assigning statistics to
every relativistic field. [A1, step 2.1, step 1.2, given] ∎

## Example

Choose a unit scalar wave-packet mode $h$ and a unit Dirac particle or
antiparticle mode $u$. The states and operators below are those of the
conditional model theorem [[pthm-qft-free-fock-statistics]].

For the bosonic mode, let $|n\rangle_h$ be the normalized $n$-occupation
vector. We also construct a normalized Fock vector whose annihilation image
is not square-summable, so the maximal annihilation operator is not defined
on every Fock vector.

For the fermionic mode, the one-particle vector
$c^\dagger(u)\Omega_D$ has unit norm, while two creations in that same mode
vanish. This calculation concerns one normalized CAR mode in the adopted
representation; it is not a general spin-statistics argument.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice [A1], the scalar mode conclusion [F1], the CAR
and exact annihilation domain [F2], and the Fock-sector definitions [F3].
The modes $h$ and $u$ are supplied unit vectors.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]] states $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

[F1] [[pthm-qft-free-fock-statistics]] proves that for each unit scalar mode
$h$, $|n\rangle_h=(a^\dagger(h))^n\Omega_s/\sqrt{n!}$ is normalized and
satisfies the bosonic ladder.

[F2] [[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]] gives the CAR
$c(u)c^\dagger(u)+c^\dagger(u)c(u)=I$ and
$c^\dagger(u)^2=0$ for a unit mode, and states that both operators are
bounded on the whole Fock space.

[F3] [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]] defines the vacuum as
$\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$, states $c(u)\Omega=0$, and gives the sector
insertion and contraction formulas. The finite-particle domain is dense.

[F4] [[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]] states the exact maximal annihilation domain
$D(a(h))=\{\Psi=(\Psi_n):\sum_{n\ge1}\|a_n(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$.

## Verification

**Given:** [A1], [F1]–[F4], and the chosen normalized modes $h$ and $u$.

1.1 Let $S_2=\sum_{k=1}^\infty k^{-2}$. For each $j\ge0$, the block
$2^j\le k<2^{j+1}$ contains $2^j$ terms, each at most $2^{-2j}$, so its
sum is at most $2^{-j}$. Summing these geometric bounds proves
$1\le S_2<\infty$. Therefore $C=S_2^{-1/2}$ is a positive finite constant,
and the orthonormal bosonic mode states from [F1] give
$\Psi=\sum_{n=0}^\infty C(n+1)^{-1}|n\rangle_h$ with
$\|\Psi\|^2=C^2S_2=1$. [A1, F1, construct, algebra]

1.2 For $\xi_n$ in the $n$th antisymmetric sector and $\eta_{n+1}$ in the
next sector, the insertion formula, $P_{a,n+1}\eta_{n+1}=\eta_{n+1}$, and
self-adjointness of this orthogonal projection give
$\langle c^\dagger_n(u)\xi_n,\eta_{n+1}\rangle_2
=\sqrt{n+1}\langle u\otimes\xi_n,\eta_{n+1}\rangle_2
=\langle\xi_n,\sqrt{n+1}(C_u\otimes I^{\otimes n})\eta_{n+1}\rangle_2
=\langle\xi_n,c_{n+1}(u)\eta_{n+1}\rangle_2$ by the tensor product pairing
and contraction formula in [F3]. Summing over finite-sector vectors proves
$\langle c^\dagger(u)\xi,\eta\rangle_2=
\langle\xi,c(u)\eta\rangle_2$ there. Boundedness in [F2] and density in [F3]
extend this identity to the full Fock space, so
$c^\dagger(u)=c(u)^*$. The CAR, vacuum relation, and nilpotence in [F2]–[F3]
then give
$\|c^\dagger(u)\Omega_D\|^2
=\langle\Omega_D,c(u)c^\dagger(u)\Omega_D\rangle_2
=\langle\Omega_D,(I-c^\dagger(u)c(u))\Omega_D\rangle_2=1$.
Thus the one-mode state is normalized and a second creation in that mode is
zero. [F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 By the ladder in [F1], the squared norm of the annihilation-sector
sequence for this vector is
$C^2\sum_{n=1}^\infty n/(n+1)^2$. Since $n+1\le2n$ for $n\ge1$,
$n/(n+1)^2\ge1/(4n)$. Each dyadic block
$2^j\le n<2^{j+1}$ contributes at least $1/2$ to the harmonic series, so

[A1, F1, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The adjoint identity and CAR in [F2] give $N_u^*=N_u$ and

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Use the finite data and notation of
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]]: $N\ge1$,
$H_N=L^2(\mathbb R^N,dq;\mathbb C)$, $D_0=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$,
and $W=V+C_0+1\ge1+c|q|^2$. For $u,v\in D_0$ define
$$a(u,v):=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\int_{\mathbb R^N}(\partial_j u)\overline{\partial_jv}\,dq+\int_{\mathbb R^N}(W+1)u\overline v\,dq,$$
and $\|u\|_Q:=a(u,u)^{1/2}$. Let $Q$ be the completion of this inner-product
space, constructed as equivalence classes of $\|\cdot\|_Q$-Cauchy sequences.
Then $Q$ is a complex Hilbert space and the map sending a Cauchy class to its
$L^2$ limit is a continuous injective linear map $Q\hookrightarrow H_N$ with
dense image. Each $u\in Q$ has weak derivatives $\partial_j u\in L^2$ and a
weighted function $\sqrt{W+1}\,u\in L^2$, and
$$\|u\|_Q^2=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+\|\sqrt{W+1}\,u\|_2^2.$$
Here $g_j=\partial_j u$ means explicitly that
$\int u\,\overline{\partial_j\varphi}=-\int g_j\overline\varphi$ for every
$\varphi\in D_0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, the data of [[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]], and the $L^2$ and density results below.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function; only countably many representatives are selected in the completion argument.

[F1] [[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]]: $H_N$ is complex $L^2$ with first-variable-linear integral pairing, $D_0=C_c^\infty$, and $W=V+C_0+1\ge1+c|q|^2$.

[F2] [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]: under Countable Choice, $H_N$ is complete for $\|\cdot\|_2$ and $\langle u,v\rangle=\int u\overline v\,dq$ is its inner product.

[F3] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]: $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$ in $H_N$.

[F4] [[thm-c-c-infinity-rn-is-dense-in-l-p-of-rn]]: under Countable Choice and for $p=2$, $D_0$ is dense in $H_N$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Since $W+1\ge2$ and every $a_j>0$, $a$ is a Hermitian positive-definite sesquilinear form on $D_0$: in particular $a(u,u)=\sum_j a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+\|\sqrt{W+1}\,u\|_2^2\ge2\|u\|_2^2$, and $a(u,u)=0$ forces $u=0$ in $H_N$. Thus its Cauchy-sequence completion with the stated equivalence relation is a well-defined inner-product space. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 To see that the completion is complete, let $(X_n)$ be a Cauchy sequence of its classes. By [A1], choose $u_n\in D_0$ with $\|[u_n]-X_n\|_Q<2^{-n}$ for each $n$. The triangle inequality makes $(u_n)$ $Q$-Cauchy; its class $X$ is defined by the Cauchy-sequence construction, and $\|X_n-X\|_Q\le2^{-n}+\|[u_n]-X\|_Q\to0$. Hence $Q$ is complete and therefore Hilbert. [A1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For a $Q$-Cauchy representative sequence $(u_n)$, the inequalities $\|u_n-u_m\|_2\le\|u_n-u_m\|_Q$, $\sqrt{a_j}\|\partial_j u_n-\partial_j u_m\|_2\le\|u_n-u_m\|_Q$, and $\|\sqrt{W+1}(u_n-u_m)\|_2\le\|u_n-u_m\|_Q$ show that $u_n$, each $\partial_j u_n$, and $\sqrt{W+1}u_n$ converge in $L^2$ by [F2]; write their limits as $u$, $g_j$, and $h$. The first limit defines a continuous map $Q\to H_N$, since $\|u\|_2\le\|[u_n]\|_Q$, and equivalent Cauchy sequences have the same $L^2$ limit. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 For every $\varphi\in D_0$, integration by parts gives $\int u_n\overline{\partial_j\varphi}=-\int (\partial_j u_n)\overline\varphi$. Passing to the limit in both integrals by $L^2$ convergence and Cauchy–Schwarz yields $\int u\overline{\partial_j\varphi}=-\int g_j\overline\varphi$, so $g_j$ is the stated weak derivative. [step 2.2, F2, F3, algebra]

3.2 On each compact ball $B_R$, the continuous polynomial $W+1$ is bounded. Therefore $\sqrt{W+1}u_n\to\sqrt{W+1}u$ in $L^2(B_R)$, while the same sequence converges there to $h$; uniqueness of limits gives $h=\sqrt{W+1}u$ almost everywhere on every integer-radius ball and hence almost everywhere on $\mathbb R^N$. Taking limits of the component norms in $a(u_n,u_n)$ now gives the displayed formula for $\|u\|_Q^2$. [step 2.2, F1, F2, algebra]

4.1 If $u=0$ in $L^2$, then step 3.1 says $\langle g_j,\varphi\rangle=0$ for every $\varphi\in D_0$; this pairing is continuous by [F3] and $D_0$ is dense by [F4], so it vanishes on all of $H_N$, and taking $\varphi=g_j$ gives $g_j=0$. Step 3.2 then gives $h=0$; the norm formula yields $\|[u_n]\|_Q=0$, so the embedding is injective. Finally its image contains $D_0$, which is dense in $H_N$ by [F4]; thus the continuous injection has dense image and all claims follow. [step 3.1, step 3.2, F3, F4, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $N\ge1$, $a_1,\ldots,a_N>0$ and $c>0$. Let
$Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ be the completion of $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$
for the form inner product
$$a_{\mathrm{osc}}(u,v):=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\int (\partial_j u)\overline{\partial_jv} +\int (c|q|^2+2)u\overline v.$$
This is the space $Q$ of
[[lem-qft-coercive-polynomial-form-domain]] for $V(q)=c|q|^2$ and $C_0=0$.
