## Statement

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), $m_o>0$ in kilograms, $\omega>0$ in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and $\hbar>0$ in $\mathrm{J\,s}$. Take the complete oscillator family $(\psi_n)_{n\ge0}$ and self-adjoint Hamiltonian $H_{\rm osc}$ of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]], with oscillator length $\ell=\sqrt{\hbar/(m_o\omega)}$ and $H_{\rm osc}\psi_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)\psi_n$. Let $\mathcal C=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_n:n\ge0\}$ be the finite Hermite span. Multiplication by position $Xf(x)=xf(x)$ maps $\mathcal C$ into itself by the Hermite recurrence. Define $U(t)$ on $\mathcal C$ by $U(t)\psi_n=e^{-i\omega(n+1/2)t}\psi_n$ and extend continuously to a unitary on the oscillator Hilbert space. For $\psi_0$ the normalized ground state, define
$$C_F(t)=\frac{m_o}{\hbar}\bigl(T X(t)X(0)\psi_0,\psi_0\bigr)_1,\qquad X(t)=U(t)^\dagger XU(t),$$
where time ordering means $T X(t)X(0)=X(t)X(0)$ for $t\ge0$ and $X(0)X(t)$ for $t<0$. Define $G_R(t)=1_{[0,\infty)}(t)\sin(\omega t)/\omega$.

Then, for every real $t$,
$$C_F(t)=\frac{e^{-i\omega|t|}}{2\omega},\qquad (\partial_t^2+\omega^2)C_F=-i\delta_0,\qquad (\partial_t^2+\omega^2)G_R=\delta_0.$$
Use the complex Schwartz space of [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]], with topology generated by $p_{jk}(\varphi)=\sup_x|x^j\varphi^{(k)}(x)|$ for integers $j,k\ge0$: a neighborhood of zero restricts finitely many such seminorms. A tempered distribution is a continuous complex-linear functional $u:\mathcal S(\mathbb R)\to\mathbb C$, with bilinear pairing $\langle u,\varphi\rangle=u(\varphi)$ (no conjugation). A bounded kernel $f$ acts by $\langle f,\varphi\rangle=\int f\varphi$. Define $\langle\partial_t^k u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^k\langle u,\varphi^{(k)}\rangle$ and $\delta_a(\varphi)=\varphi(a)$. These derivatives also restrict to compactly supported smooth tests. Convergence of distributions here means convergence against every Schwartz test, the weak topology $\sigma(\mathcal S',\mathcal S)$. For $u\in\mathcal S'$ define its positive-sign Fourier transform by $\langle\mathcal T_+u,\varphi\rangle=\langle u,\mathcal T_+\varphi\rangle$, where $\mathcal T_+\varphi(t)=\int e^{i\nu t}\varphi(\nu)\,d\nu$. Both kernels have units of seconds, so the differential identities have units of inverse seconds. In particular, $C_F(t)\ne0$ for $t<0$ while $G_R(t)=0$ there.

For a Schwartz test function $\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$ and $\epsilon>0$, define $\operatorname{PV}\int\varphi(x)/x\,dx:=\lim_{r\downarrow0}\int_{|x|>r}\varphi(x)/x\,dx$ and $\delta_a(\varphi):=\varphi(a)$. The Plemelj boundary identity is
$$\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\varphi(x)}{x+i\epsilon}\,dx =\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\varphi(x)}x\,dx-i\pi\varphi(0),$$
with the opposite sign of $i\epsilon$ reversing the delta sign. In this boundary formula $x$ and $\epsilon$ use one common coordinate unit. For $\nu\in\mathbb R$ in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, the frequency regulator $\epsilon>0$ is in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ and $\epsilon t$ is dimensionless; the ordinary positive-sign Fourier transform of $e^{-\epsilon|t|}C_F(t)$ is
$$\frac{i}{2\omega}\left(\frac1{\nu-\omega+i\epsilon}-\frac1{\nu+\omega-i\epsilon}\right).$$
As $\epsilon\downarrow0$ its distributional limit is
$$\frac{i}{2\omega}\left[ \operatorname{PV}\frac1{\nu-\omega}-\operatorname{PV}\frac1{\nu+\omega} -i\pi\delta_{\omega}-i\pi\delta_{-\omega}\right],$$
which is conventionally denoted $i/(\nu^2-\omega^2+i0)$. Here that notation means the displayed pair of opposite boundary values at the two simple poles. This one-mode result makes no spatial-causality or interacting-field claim.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, $m_o,\omega,\hbar>0$ with units as stated, the published oscillator Hamiltonian and basis, and the time-ordered product on the core $\mathcal C$.

[F1] [[def-qft-example-data]]: energy, time, mass, action, and Hilbert-pairing conventions are as stated; in particular $\omega t$ is dimensionless and the pairing is first-variable-linear.

Rescaling [F3] gives $$X\psi_n=\sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2m_o\omega}}\left(\sqrt n\,\psi_{n-1}+\sqrt{n+1}\,\psi_{n+1}\right),$$ with $\psi_{-1}=0$. Thus $X$ maps the finite span $\mathcal C$ into itself, so all products in the statement are defined on $\psi_0$. On a finite vector $\sum_{n=0}^Nc_n\psi_n$, the phase rule preserves norm by orthonormality [F11]; its inverse is the opposite phase rule. Density of $\mathcal C$ follows from completeness in [F11], and Hilbert completeness [F12] gives unique continuous extensions of both inverse isometries to the whole oscillator Hilbert space. Hence $U(t)$ is unitary and agrees on $\mathcal C$ with the energy evolution [F2]. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, F10, F11, F12, algebra]

1.2 Fix $\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$. Set $\chi=1_{[-1,1]}$ and $\psi=\varphi-\varphi(0)\chi$. The function $\chi$ is even and integrable, $\psi(0)=0$, and $\psi(x)/x$ is bounded near zero because $\chi=1$ there and $\varphi$ is differentiable. Outside $[-1,1]$, $\psi=\varphi$, so $\psi(x)/x$ is integrable at infinity; on compact sets away from zero it is also integrable. For any integrable complex $q$, put $I=\int q$. If $I=0$, $|I|\le\int|q|$ is immediate; otherwise $\alpha=\overline I/|I|$ gives $|I|=\int\operatorname{Re}(\alpha q)\le\int|q|$. Decompose the regularized integral as $R_\epsilon-iJ_\epsilon$, where $R_\epsilon=\int x\varphi(x)/(x^2+\epsilon^2)\,dx$ and $J_\epsilon=\int\epsilon\varphi(x)/(x^2+\epsilon^2)\,dx$. These are complex kernel contributions, not scalar real and imaginary parts. The first contribution is $$\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{x\psi(x)}{x^2+\epsilon^2}\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\psi(x)}x\,\frac{x^2}{x^2+\epsilon^2}\,dx,$$ because the omitted $\varphi(0)\chi$ term is odd. For $0<r<1$, the error from replacing $x^2/(x^2+\epsilon^2)$ by $1$ on $|x|<r$ is at most $2r p_{01}(\varphi)$, since $|\psi(x)/x|\le p_{01}(\varphi)$ there (assign its derivative limit at $x=0$). On $|x|\ge r$, the error is at most $(\epsilon^2/r^2)\|\psi/x\|_1$. Given $\eta>0$, choose a fixed $r\in(0,1)$ such that $2r p_{01}(\varphi)<\eta/2$; then choose $\epsilon_0>0$ such that $(\epsilon_0^2/r^2)\|\psi/x\|_1<\eta/2$. The total error is below $\eta$ for every $0<\epsilon<\epsilon_0$, proving convergence to $\int\psi(x)/x\,dx$. Since $\operatorname{PV}\int\chi(x)/x\,dx=0$, this is $\operatorname{PV}\int\varphi(x)/x\,dx$. Moreover its limiting action is continuous: $|\int\psi/x|\le2p_{01}(\varphi)+p_{20}(\varphi)$, by the derivative bound on $|x|<1$ and the tail bound $|\varphi(x)/x|\le p_{20}(\varphi)|x|^{-3}$ for $|x|>1$. Thus the principal value is a tempered distribution. [given, F4, algebra]

2.1 The second kernel contribution is $-iJ_\epsilon=-i\int\varphi(x)\epsilon/(x^2+\epsilon^2)\,dx$. The nonnegative kernel has integral $\pi$, by the antiderivative $\arctan(x/\epsilon)$. For any $r>0$, continuity bounds the error from replacing $\varphi(x)$ by $\varphi(0)$ on $|x|\le r$ by $\pi\sup_{|x|\le r}|\varphi(x)-\varphi(0)|$. On $|x|>r$, the kernel mass is at most $2\epsilon/r$, so the error is at most $4\|\varphi\|_\infty\epsilon/r$. First choose $r$ small and then $\epsilon$ small. This proves $J_\epsilon\to\pi\varphi(0)$ and hence $R_\epsilon-iJ_\epsilon\to\operatorname{PV}\int\varphi(x)/x\,dx-i\pi\varphi(0)$ for complex tests. Replacing $+i\epsilon$ by $-i\epsilon$ changes the second contribution to $+iJ_\epsilon$ and reverses the delta sign. Evaluation is continuous since $|\varphi(0)|\le p_{00}(\varphi)$. [given, F4, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 Put $d_o=\sqrt{\hbar/(2m_o\omega)}$. From step 1.1, $X\psi_0=d_o\psi_1$ and $X\psi_1=d_o(\psi_0+\sqrt2\,\psi_2)$. Multiplying by $m_o/\hbar$ and using $m_od_o^2/\hbar=1/(2\omega)$ proves $C_F(t)=e^{-i\omega|t|}/(2\omega)$. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, F10, algebra]

3.1 For $\epsilon>0$, the damped kernel is integrable, and its positive-sign Fourier transform is the sum of two ordinary half-line integrals: $$\int_{\mathbb R}e^{i\nu t}e^{-\epsilon|t|}C_F(t)\,dt=\frac1{2\omega}\left(\frac1{\epsilon+i(\omega-\nu)}+\frac1{\epsilon+i(\omega+\nu)}\right)=\frac{i}{2\omega}\left(\frac1{\nu-\omega+i\epsilon}-\frac1{\nu+\omega-i\epsilon}\right).$$ The first equality follows by integrating $e^{-(\epsilon+i(\omega-\nu))t}$ on $t\ge0$ and $e^{-(\epsilon+i(\omega+\nu))|t|}$ on $t<0$; both real decay rates are $\epsilon>0$. [given, F5, F8, F9, step 2.2, algebra]

3.2 All bounded kernels used here are tempered: $|\int f\varphi|\le2\|f\|_\infty(p_{00}(\varphi)+p_{20}(\varphi))$. Derivative actions are continuous because $p_{jk}(\varphi^{(r)})=p_{j,k+r}(\varphi)$. The function $C_F$ is continuous at $0$, solves $C_F''+\omega^2C_F=0$ classically on each open half-line, and has one-sided derivatives $C_F'(0+)= -i/2$ and $C_F'(0-)= i/2$. For a test $\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$, integrate $\int_{-\infty}^0 C_F\varphi''+\int_0^\infty C_F\varphi''$ by parts twice; rapid decay of the test and its derivative removes the boundary terms at infinity. The boundary terms in $\varphi'(0)$ cancel because $C_F$ is continuous; the remaining coefficient of $\varphi(0)$ is $C_F'(0+)-C_F'(0-)=-i$. Thus $(\partial_t^2+\omega^2)C_F=-i\delta_0$. [given, step 2.2, algebra]

3.3 The function $G_R$ is zero on $t<0$, solves $G_R''+\omega^2G_R=0$ on $t>0$, is continuous at zero with $G_R(0)=0$, and has derivative jump $G_R'(0+)-G_R'(0-)=1$. The same two integrations by parts show $(\partial_t^2+\omega^2)G_R=\delta_0$. Since $C_F(t)$ has modulus $1/(2\omega)>0$ for $t<0$ but $G_R(t)=0$ there, the Feynman kernel is not the retarded response. [given, step 2.2, F10, algebra]

4.1 To justify the distribution limit, the Fourier transform in [F6] and the rescaling in [F5] preserve the Schwartz test space. The time-side kernels $e^{-\epsilon|t|}C_F(t)$ converge to $C_F$ against every such transformed test: on $|t|\le R$, $|e^{-\epsilon|t|}-1|\le\epsilon R$, and the tail is bounded by $(1/\omega)\int_{|t|>R}|\mathcal T_+\varphi(t)|dt$, which tends to zero as $R\to\infty$. Applying the Plemelj limits in steps 1.2 and 2.1 to the two shifted poles gives the displayed boundary distribution. Combining the rational terms at finite $\epsilon$ gives $(i+\epsilon/\omega)/(\nu^2-\omega^2+2i\epsilon\omega+\epsilon^2)$, so the numerator tends to $i$ and the two poles approach from opposite sides. In the $i0$ shorthand, the exact partial-fraction definition is $$\frac{i}{\nu^2-\omega^2+i0}:=\frac{i}{2\omega}\left(\frac1{\nu-\omega+i0}-\frac1{\nu+\omega-i0}\right),$$ where each $i0$ is the boundary proved above; the opposite sign at the second pole follows from $\nu^2-\omega^2=(\nu-\omega)(\nu+\omega)$ and $\omega>0$. No contour integration or unproved pole rule is used. [given, F5, F6, F7, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

A **formal coefficient graph** here is a finite directed graph of interaction
vertices and internal lines with a momentum covector assigned to each line and
momentum conservation imposed at each vertex. It records a coefficient at a
fixed finite or formal order; it is not, by this definition, a convergent

## Postulate

Adopt the following specified free-photon model in the oriented,
time-oriented affine Minkowski spacetime and length coordinates of
[[def-qft-framework-units]], with metric $(-,+,+,+)$ and $x^0=ct$. The
classical electromagnetic input is the smooth source-free branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]; the electromagnetic two-form and its potential
components are those of [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]], and a supplied
potential is subject to [[def-em-gauge-transformation]]. These EM suppliers

For almost every $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, set
$\mathbf n=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and
$P_T(\mathbf k)=I_3-\mathbf n\mathbf n^{\mathsf T}$. The mathematical
definition [[def-qft-photon-transverse-space]] specifies the positive
one-photon Hilbert space

$$\mathcal H_T= \{u\in L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^3): \mathbf k\cdot u(\mathbf k)=0\text{ for almost every }\mathbf k\},$$

with the inherited pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_2=\int\overline{u(\mathbf k)}\cdot v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k$,
linear in the second variable as in [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. The

continuous polarization frame over all momentum directions is chosen. Adopt
the bosonic Fock representation $\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_T)$ and the free

$$H_\gamma=\hbar c\,d\Gamma(|\mathbf k|),$$

where on the $n$-photon sector $d\Gamma(|\mathbf k|)$ is multiplication by

constructed in [[lem-qft-photon-local-weyl-observables]]; a pointwise

For the physical interpretation of an actually constructed state and a

## Statement

This is a conditional mathematical theorem about the prescribed current and
free coherent-state construction defined below, under the exact supplier
interfaces [F2] and [L1]. Here “soft current” is only a name for the displayed
rational function: no scattering-amplitude factorization or approximation
claim is made. The weak-zero and no-strong-limit conclusions are conditional
on [L1]; the projective-ray conclusion is proved separately in step 7.1.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the constants and conventions of
[[def-qft-example-data]], and that the two supplier interfaces [F2]
and [L1] hold exactly as stated below. Let $I$ be a finite, possibly empty,
set of leg labels. A leg $i\in I$ carries an energy $E_i>0$ in joules,
a dimensionless velocity $v_i=\mathbf v_{i,\rm phys}/c\in\mathbb R^3$ with
$\mathbf v_{i,\rm phys}$ in m s$^{-1}$ and
$|v_i|<1$, a dimensionless charge number $Q_i\in\mathbb R$ (physical charge
$eQ_i$ coulombs), and an orientation sign $\eta_i\in\{-1,1\}$, with
$\eta_i=-1$ for an incoming leg and $+1$ for an outgoing leg. Require charge
balance $\sum_{i\in I}\eta_iQ_i=0$. Use
$h=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$ and
$h(a,b)=a^0b^0-\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b$ for algebraic four-vector
contractions. For $n\in S^2:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|=1\}$ and energy
$\omega>0$ in joules, put
$$ p_i=E_i(1,v_i),\qquad q=\omega(1,n),\qquad K:S^2\to\mathbb R^4,\quad K(n)=\sum_{i\in I}\eta_iQ_i\frac{(1,v_i)}{1-v_i\cdot n}. $$
Each $p_i$ has positive energy and
$h(p_i,p_i)=E_i^2(1-|v_i|^2)>0$; this timelike condition is the precise
meaning of “massive” here, with rest mass
$m_i=E_i\sqrt{1-|v_i|^2}/c^2>0$. The prescribed current is the function
$J(q)=\sum_{i\in I}\eta_iQ_i\,p_i/h(p_i,q)$ on
$\{\omega(1,n):\omega>0,\ n\in S^2\}$. Since
$h(p_i,q)=E_i\omega(1-v_i\cdot n)>0$, this equals $K(n)/\omega$.
Thus $K$ is dimensionless and $J(q)$ has units $\mathrm J^{-1}$.
Write $K(n)=(K^0(n),\mathbf K(n))$, let $P_T(n)=I-n\otimes n$, and
$K_\perp(n)=P_T(n)\mathbf K(n)$. Define $d\Omega$ as Euclidean chart
surface measure on $S^2$ and
$$ C=\frac{g^2}{2(2\pi)^3}\int_{S^2}|K_\perp(n)|^2\,d\Omega(n)\ge0. $$
Here $g>0$ is the dimensionless coupling of [[def-qft-example-data]] and
$\lambda,\Lambda$ are energy cutoffs in joules. Write $\mathbf q=\omega n$
for the spatial energy coordinate, distinct from the four-vector
$q=(\omega,\mathbf q)$ above. For $\mathbf q\ne0$, put $\omega=|\mathbf q|$
and $n=\mathbf q/|\mathbf q|$ and define
$$ h_\lambda(\mathbf q)=g\frac{K_\perp(n)}{\omega}\mathbf1_{\{\lambda<\omega<\Lambda\}},\qquad 0<\lambda<\Lambda; $$
Set $h_\lambda(0)=0$ and regard $h_\lambda$ as a function of $\mathbf q$.
Define
$\mathcal H_{E,T}:=\{h\in L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf q/[(2\pi)^3 2|\mathbf q|];\mathbb C^3):\mathbf q\cdot h(\mathbf q)=0\ {\rm a.e.}\}$,
with the componentwise Hermitian integral pairing linear in its second
variable. On this energy-coordinate transverse Hilbert space the exact norm is
$$ N_\lambda=\|h_\lambda\|^2=C\log(\Lambda/\lambda). $$
The energy-coordinate wavefunction has units $\mathrm J^{-1}$ and its
one-particle measure has units $\mathrm J^2$, so $N_\lambda$ and $C$ are
dimensionless; its value at $q=0$ is immaterial to this $L^2$ vector.
Under the canonical unitary $U:\mathcal H_{E,T}\to\mathcal H_T$ specified and proved in step 3.1,
the same vector is represented by the length-coordinate vector $f_\lambda$
defined as follows. Set $f_\lambda(0)=0$ and, for $k\ne0$, define
$$ f_\lambda(k)=\mathbf1_{\{\lambda/(\hbar c)<|k|<\Lambda/(\hbar c)\}} |k|^{-3/2}b(k/|k|),\qquad b(n)=\frac{gK_\perp(n)}{\sqrt{2(2\pi)^3}},\qquad \int_{S^2}|b|^2\,d\Omega=C. $$
Here $b$ is dimensionless and the $L^2(d^3k)$ wavefunction $f_\lambda$ has
units $\mathrm m^{3/2}$.
The normalized coherent vector
$\Psi_\lambda=W(-i\sqrt2 f_\lambda)\Omega
=\exp(-N_\lambda/2)\epsilon(f_\lambda)$ has squared norm in sector $m$
$$ s_m=\exp(-N_\lambda)\frac{N_\lambda^m}{m!},\qquad \sum_{m\ge0}s_m=1,\qquad \sum_{m\ge0}m s_m=N_\lambda, $$
with $N_\lambda^0=1$ also when $N_\lambda=0$.
These are Hilbert-space sector norms and their index sum; no measured
probability is asserted. For the free photon energy operator
$H_\gamma=\hbar c\,d\Gamma(|k|)$, $\Psi_\lambda$ is in its operator domain
and its quadratic expectation is $C(\Lambda-\lambda)$ joules.

If $C=0$, $f_\lambda=0$ almost everywhere and $\Psi_\lambda=\Omega$ for each
cutoff. If $C>0$, the exact hypotheses of the current [L1] hold with
$\epsilon=\lambda/(\hbar c)$, $\kappa=\Lambda/(\hbar c)$ and the displayed
nonzero transverse angular function $b$. Conditional on [L1], the family has
no strong Fock-vector limit and converges weakly to zero, while its free
energy expectation stays bounded. For a unit Fock vector $u$, define its
projective ray $[u]:=\{zu:z\in\mathbb C,\ |z|=1\}$. For unit vectors $u,v$
define their projective-ray distance by
$d([u],[v]):=\inf_{|z|=1}\|u-zv\|$. This is a metric on phase classes: symmetry follows by replacing $z$ with
$\overline z$, the triangle inequality follows from the norm triangle
inequality and phase invariance, and compactness of the unit circle makes zero
distance equivalent to equality of the classes. Projective convergence means convergence in this
distance, equivalently norm convergence to a fixed unit vector after allowing
a unit-modulus phase at each cutoff. Step 7.1 proves separately that
these rays have no projective limit, including after arbitrary phase choices. This is
not a result about full interacting QED, universal charged sectors,
detector-inclusive observables, or measured photon statistics.

$1-v_i\cdot n\ge1-|v_i|>0$. Since the leg set is finite, each summand of
$K(n)$ is continuous and bounded on $S^2$. Moreover
$$ h(K(n),(1,n))= \sum_i\eta_iQ_i\frac{1-v_i\cdot n}{1-v_i\cdot n} =\sum_i\eta_iQ_i=0. $$
Thus $K^0(n)=n\cdot\mathbf K(n)$ and
$h(K,K)=(K^0)^2-|\mathbf K|^2=-|P_T(n)\mathbf K(n)|^2$.
Consequently the angular integrand is nonnegative, bounded and measurable;
the coefficient $C$ is finite and nonnegative. [given, A1, F1, algebra]

1.2 By [F10] at $p=2$, the real-valued scalar space $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R)$ has a countable dense set $D$. It is nonempty because this scalar $L^2$ space is nonempty and $D$ is dense. By [F12], $D\times D$ is at most countable; [F14] supplies a surjection from $\mathbb N$ onto this nonempty product. Composing with $(d,e)\mapsto d+ie$ and applying [F14] again shows that $D_{\mathbb C}:=\{d+ie:d,e\in D\}$ is at most countable. For every complex scalar $u\in L^2$, its real and imaginary parts $u_R,u_I$ belong to real $L^2$, and $\|u-(d+ie)\|_2^2=\|u_R-d\|_2^2+\|u_I-e\|_2^2$; density of $D$ therefore makes $D_{\mathbb C}$ dense in complex scalar $L^2$. By two applications of [F12], $D_{\mathbb C}^3$ is countable and dense in $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$, since each of three components can be approximated with squared error below $\varepsilon^2/3$. For $n\in S^2$ and $z\in\mathbb C^3$, put $a=\sum_j n_jz_j$. Using [F13] and the reality of $n_j$, direct expansion gives $\|P_T(n)z\|^2=\sum_j|z_j-n_ja|^2=\sum_j|z_j|^2-|a|^2\le\|z\|^2$, and $(I-nn^T)^2=I-nn^T$. Its image of $D_{\mathbb C}^3$ is countable and dense in its range: for $z=M_{P_T}z$ choose $w\in D_{\mathbb C}^3$ close to $z$, and $\|M_{P_T}w-z\|_2\le\|w-z\|_2$. [A1, F2, F10, F12, F13, F14]

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert
space, and let $N$, $E_N(B)$, and $P_n$ be as in
[[def-qft-x03-photon-count-pvm]]. Then $N$ is self-adjoint on its stated
domain and $E_N$ is a projection-valued measure on the Borel subsets of
$\mathbb R$. It is the sector counting resolution: $E_N(B)$ keeps exactly the
sectors whose integer label lies in $B$, and $N$ multiplies sector $n$ by $n$.
For any finite Borel partition $(B_a)_{a=1}^m$ of $\mathbb R$, the projections
$E_N(B_a)$ are mutually orthogonal and sum to the identity.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, the square-summable symmetric Fock direct sum,
the number-operator definition, and the standard definitions of adjoint,
self-adjoint operator, and projection-valued measure.

[A1] Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]] is the choice assumption of
the Fock construction used here.

[F1] [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]: $\mathcal F_s(H)$ is the Hilbert direct
sum of the symmetric sectors $H_s^{(n)}$, $n\ge0$, with
$\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty$; finite-sector vectors form a dense subspace.

[F2] [[def-qft-x03-photon-count-pvm]]: $D(N)=\{\Psi:\sum_n n^2\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$,
$(N\Psi)_n=n\Psi_n$, and $(E_N(B)\Psi)_n=\mathbf1_B(n)\Psi_n$.

[F3] [[def-projection-valued-measure]]: every value must be an orthogonal
projection, $E_N(\varnothing)=0$, $E_N(\mathbb R)=I$,
$E_N(B\cap C)=E_N(B)E_N(C)$, and disjoint countable unions must converge
strongly.

[F4] Under the second-variable-linear Fock pairing of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], conjugating the first-variable-linear
definition in [[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]] gives:
$y\in D(N^*)$ exactly when there is $z$ such that
$\langle Nx,y\rangle_2=\langle x,z\rangle_2$ for every $x\in D(N)$; then
$N^*y=z$.

[F5] [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]:
self-adjointness means equality of the operator and its adjoint, including
equality of their domains.

## Proof

**Given:** [A1], [F1]–[F5], and the number-operator and sector-projection
formulas in [F2].

1.1 Finite-sector vectors lie in $D(N)$ and are dense by [F1]. For $\Psi,\Phi\in D(N)$, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives absolute convergence of $\sum_n n\langle\Psi_n,\Phi_n\rangle_2$, and because each $n$ is real, $$\langle N\Psi,\Phi\rangle_2 =\sum_n n\langle\Psi_n,\Phi_n\rangle_2 =\langle\Psi,N\Phi\rangle_2.$$ Thus $N$ is densely defined and symmetric. [A1, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 For each Borel $B$, [F2] makes $E_N(B)$ the diagonal multiplier by the real indicator $\mathbf1_B(n)$. It is bounded with norm at most one, self-adjoint, and idempotent. The same coordinate formula gives $E_N(\varnothing)=0$, $E_N(\mathbb R)=I$, and $E_N(B)E_N(C)=E_N(B\cap C)$. [F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Suppose $y\in D(N^*)$ and write $z=N^*y$. Test [F4] on vectors supported in only sector $n$. Since $N$ acts there as $nI$, the identity for every $x_n\in H_s^{(n)}$ gives $z_n=ny_n$. Hence $\sum_n n^2\|y_n\|^2=\sum_n\|z_n\|^2<\infty$, so $y\in D(N)$ and $N^*y=Ny$. Conversely, if $y\in D(N)$, the convergent sector sum in step 1.1 gives $\langle Nx,y\rangle_2=\langle x,Ny\rangle_2$ for every $x\in D(N)$; [F4] then gives $y\in D(N^*)$ and $N^*y=Ny$. Thus $D(N^*)=D(N)$ and $N=N^*$, which proves self-adjointness by [F5]. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Let $(B_j)_{j\ge0}$ be pairwise disjoint Borel sets with union $B$, and fix $\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H)$. Given $\epsilon>0$, choose $M$ so that $\sum_{n>M}\|\Psi_n\|^2<\epsilon$. Among the finitely many labels $0,\ldots,M$, each label in $B$ belongs to one $B_j$; choose $J$ at least as large as all those finitely many indices. Then $E_N(B)\Psi-\sum_{j=0}^{J}E_N(B_j)\Psi$ has zero components through sector $M$, and its squared norm is at most $\sum_{n>M}\|\Psi_n\|^2<\epsilon$. This proves strong countable additivity. Together with step 1.2 it proves the PVM clauses in [F3]. The coordinate formula in [F2] shows this PVM retains exactly the sectors on which $N$ acts by their labels. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 In a finite Borel partition $(B_a)_{a=1}^m$ of $\mathbb R$, distinct sets are disjoint, so step 1.2 gives $E_N(B_a)E_N(B_b)=0$ for $a\ne b$. Append empty sets to this finite list to apply the countable-additivity result of step 2.2; since the union is $\mathbb R$ and $E_N(\mathbb R)=I$, the finite projections sum to $I$. [F3, step 1.2, step 2.2] ∎

Let $m>0$ be a particle mass in kilograms, $q\in\mathbb R$ its charge in coulombs, and $A:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ a smooth spatial vector potential with components in tesla-metres. Use standard Cartesian coordinates $x_i$ measured in metres and write $\partial_i:=\partial/\partial x_i$. Let $\epsilon_{ijk}$ be the alternating symbol with $\epsilon_{123}=1$, and sum repeated spatial indices from $1$ to $3$. Define $B_k(x)=\epsilon_{kij}\partial_iA_j(x)$ and $\mathbf B=(B_1,B_2,B_3):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$; its smooth components are in tesla.

Let $\mathcal C=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^4)$ be the common invariant test domain. In this item, “common core” refers only to this shared domain of the displayed differential expressions; no operator-theoretic core property for a closure is asserted. Define the dimensionless finite matrices
$$\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},$$
$$\beta=\begin{pmatrix}I_2&0\\0&-I_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad \alpha_i=\begin{pmatrix}0&\sigma_i\\\sigma_i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \Sigma_i=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_i,\sigma_i),$$
and use $\hbar,c$ of [[def-qft-example-data]]. On $\mathcal C$, define
$$\pi_i\psi=-i\hbar\partial_i\psi-qA_i\psi,\qquad H_D\psi=c\sum_{i=1}^3\alpha_i\pi_i\psi+\beta mc^2\psi.$$
These maps preserve $\mathcal C$. The components $\pi_i$ have units $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$ and $H_D$ has units joules. Define the operator expressions
$$\boldsymbol\pi^2\psi:=\sum_{i=1}^3\pi_i(\pi_i\psi),\qquad (\boldsymbol\Sigma\cdot\mathbf B)\psi:=\sum_{i=1}^3\Sigma_iB_i\psi.$$
Here $[\pi_i,\pi_j]:=\pi_i\circ\pi_j-\pi_j\circ\pi_i$, and $H_D^2$ denotes composition on $\mathcal C$. On $\mathcal C$, the identities are
$$[\pi_i,\pi_j]=iq\hbar\epsilon_{ijk}B_k,\qquad H_D^2=m^2c^4I_4+c^2(\boldsymbol\pi^2-q\hbar\boldsymbol\Sigma\cdot\mathbf B).$$
The operator $K:=\boldsymbol\pi^2-q\hbar\boldsymbol\Sigma\cdot\mathbf B$ maps $\mathcal C$ to itself and has units $(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}})^2$.

For commuting formal indeterminates $t,X$ over $\mathbb R$, define the first-order square-root coefficient $a$ by
$$(mc^2+taX)^2\equiv m^2c^4+tc^2X\pmod{t^2}.$$
Comparing the coefficient of $tX$ gives $a=1/(2m)$; substituting $K$ for $X$ gives the formal first-degree correction $K/(2m)$, with no operator square-root assertion. Its spin term is $-(q/m)\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf B$, where $S_i=\hbar\Sigma_i/2$, $\mathbf S=(S_1,S_2,S_3)$, and $(\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf B)\psi:=\sum_{i=1}^3S_iB_i\psi$. The magnetic-moment dot product below uses the same componentwise sum convention.

Under the coefficient convention $H_{\mathrm{mag}}=-\boldsymbol\mu_{\mathrm{mag}}\cdot\mathbf B$ and $\boldsymbol\mu_{\mathrm{mag}}=g_s(q/(2m))\mathbf S$, equality of the formal coefficients as a linear function of $q$ gives $g_s=2$ for the minimal tree-level term. Here $H_{\mathrm{mag}}$ has units joules and $\boldsymbol\mu_{\mathrm{mag}}$ has units $\mathrm{A\,m^2}$. No magnetic self-adjoint closure, full spectrum, operator square-root theorem, radiative correction, or empirical prediction is asserted.

## Proof

1.1 For $\psi\in\mathcal C$, expand $\pi_i\pi_j\psi-\pi_j\pi_i\psi$. The second derivatives and products $A_iA_j$ cancel; the remaining derivative terms are $iq\hbar(\partial_iA_j-\partial_jA_i)\psi=iq\hbar\epsilon_{ijk}B_k\psi$ by the stated alternating-symbol and summation conventions. Smoothness of $A$ ensures each multiplication and differentiation maps $\mathcal C$ to itself. [given, F2, algebra]

1.2 In $\mathbb R[X,t]/(t^2)$, the coefficient of $tX$ in $(mc^2+taX)^2$ is $2mc^2a$. The defining identity in the Statement sets this equal to $c^2$, so $a=1/(2m)$ since $m>0$. Substituting $K$ for $X$, the spin part of $K/(2m)$ is $-q\hbar\boldsymbol\Sigma\cdot\mathbf B/(2m)=-(q/m)\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf B$. [given, algebra]

2.1 Direct multiplication of the displayed $2\times2$ matrices gives $\sigma_i^2=I_2$, $\sigma_1\sigma_2=i\sigma_3$, $\sigma_2\sigma_3=i\sigma_1$, and $\sigma_3\sigma_1=i\sigma_2$; each reversed product has the opposite sign. Thus $\sigma_i\sigma_j=\delta_{ij}I_2+i\epsilon_{ijk}\sigma_k$. Block multiplication gives $\alpha_i\alpha_j=\delta_{ij}I_4+i\epsilon_{ijk}\Sigma_k$, $\alpha_i\beta=-\beta\alpha_i$, and $\beta^2=I_4$. These fixed constant matrices commute with every $\pi_j$. Expand $(\sum_i\alpha_i\pi_i)^2=\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_j\pi_i\pi_j$. The $\delta_{ij}$ term in the derived block product is the operator $\boldsymbol\pi^2$ defined in the Statement. Its antisymmetric term is
$$\frac{i}{2}\epsilon_{ijk}\Sigma_k[\pi_i,\pi_j] =-\frac{q\hbar}{2}\epsilon_{ijk}\epsilon_{ij\ell}\Sigma_kB_\ell =-q\hbar\boldsymbol\Sigma\cdot\mathbf B,$$
because $\epsilon_{ijk}\epsilon_{ij\ell}=2\delta_{k\ell}$. The cross terms with $\beta mc^2$ cancel by $\alpha_i\beta+\beta\alpha_i=0$, and $\beta^2=I_4$. This proves the displayed square identity on $\mathcal C$; no product outside that domain is used. [step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 The coefficient of the term linear in $q$ is $-(q/m)\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf B$. Equating it with $-g_s(q/(2m))\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf B$ as a formal coefficient identity gives $g_s=2$, including the zero-charge specialization of that identity. This is only a formal lowest-order coefficient comparison, not an operator or empirical conclusion. [step 1.2, given, algebra] ∎
